question_view.question_text:
A recent study has found that those businesses which engaged more with social media had more financial success than businesses which did not. The businesses which were the most engaged saw their revenue grow by 18 per cent over the last year, while the least engaged saw losses of 8 per cent. Since social media is the future of communication, it can be seen that businesses should interact more with social media in order to maximise their profits.
Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

main_body.text: A recent study has found that those businesses which engaged more with social media had more financial success than businesses which did not. The businesses which were the most engaged saw their revenue grow by 18 per cent over the last year, while the least engaged saw losses of 8 per cent. Since social media is the future of communication, it can be seen that businesses should interact more with social media in order to maximise their profits.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: It ignores the fact that not all businesses use social media.

options.label: B
options.text: It assumes that businesses that do not use social media will collapse.

options.label: C
options.text: It assumes that participation in social media causes an increase in profits.

options.label: D
options.text: It ignores the fact that businesses can use other forms of communication.

options.label: E
options.text: It assumes that a growth in revenue of 18 per cent is possible for all businesses.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
When dealing with this kind of question, first try to summarise the steps of the
argument. Then look at how each step leads on to the next and try to identify the
flaw. The argument in question is that social media increases revenue. Since social
media will become big in the future, it must be utilised to maximise profits. The
key flaw in this question is that revenue is used interchangeably with profits.
While social media use seems to increase revenue, it is wrong to assume that it
increases profits. The answer is therefore C.
Let us look at why the other answer choices are wrong:

items.text:
A- the argument states that if a business uses social media, its profits increase.

The apostrophe has limited usefulness as a punctuation mark, so it will be no loss if it disappears altogether from the English language. The fact that it can’t be heard at all in speech suggests we can make our meaning clear without it. It is already disappearing from much business correspondence without commerce grinding to a halt. The apostrophe is also widely misused, which is surely another measure of its unimportance. Many people apparently think it belongs in any word that ends with an ‘s’, as demonstrated by this sign seen in an off-licence window: ‘Beer’s, wine’s and spirit’s at pre-budget price’s’. Yet judging by the queue in the shop, nobody had failed to get the message that there were bargains to be had.

blocks.text:
This question clearly has a straightforward approach: calculate the cost for all
possible combinations and choose the cheapest. This is going to be time intensive
and we must find a quick way of doing it for the TSA. The younger sister will only
be three years old and so gets free entry. This means that they can be completely
ignored for the purposes of calculating the minimal cost. This leaves: one
employed adult, one unemployed adult, one senior citizen, one senior citizen
spectator and two children. The party is happening on a Saturday afternoon so
this is clearly going to be during peak hours. With only two children, we can get
one spectator ticket so we need to figure out how to get this ticket to minimize
cost. Spectators have the lowest ticket cost so it makes sense to pay 70p for a
spectator ticket. We can then either get the mum an adult ticket (£3.80) and a
concession family ticket (£4.80) or we can get the grandpa a senior citizen ticket
(£1.90) and a family ticket (£9.50). These give a total cost of £9.30 and £12.10
respectively. The previous is therefore the minimal cost. This was quite arduous
and not fully rigorous but a rigor is not needed for the TSA.

Some say that religion is crucial for providing us with a moral framework, for giving clear strong moral guidance. Without religion, some say, people might lose their sense of morality altogether. But those who argue this ought to consider the Ancient Greeks. The Greeks pondered obsessively the question of what makes a good life and how to live well. In fact the word ‘ethics’ comes from them. And although they had their own set of gods, those gods were hardly moral role models (Zeus himself was a serial adulterer). Moreover, there was nothing by way of an agreed religious text from which to obtain their moral rules. There was even an atheist movement in Ancient Greece. The Greeks alone are proof that if we are to lose our faith in God, this does not mean we must also lose our faith in morality.
Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

Most European countries would not tolerate the presence of huge, wild, man-eating cats roaming wild in the countryside, decimating their profits and killing their children. question_view.question_text:
It is both morally and economically wrong for the Government to give implicit approval to an employment system that lands the state with a huge bill to top up the incomes of the lowest earners. The holes in millions of pay cheques are being plugged by in-work support to the tune of £4 bn a year. But why aren’t those who are profiting from their workers paying up? Why is the Government having to subsidise businesses who don’t pay their employees enough to live on? It is a question we need to answer and act on – fast. The cost of living is rising but wages are not. In the rush for profit, and for high pay at the top, too many companies have forgotten the basic moral imperative that employees be paid enough to live on.
Which one of the following is the best statement of the principle underlying the above argument?

main_body.text: It is both morally and economically wrong for the Government to give implicit approval to an employment system that lands the state with a huge bill to top up the incomes of the lowest earners. The holes in millions of pay cheques are being plugged by in-work support to the tune of £4 bn a year. But why aren’t those who are profiting from their workers paying up? Why is the Government having to subsidise businesses who don’t pay their employees enough to live on? It is a question we need to answer and act on – fast. The cost of living is rising but wages are not. In the rush for profit, and for high pay at the top, too many companies have forgotten the basic moral imperative that employees be paid enough to live on.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is the best statement of the principle underlying the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The Government is responsible for the employment system that leaves holes in millions of pay cheques.

options.label: B
options.text: It is morally wrong of the Government to assist people on low incomes.

options.label: C
options.text: High pay at the top end is responsible for low wages at the bottom end of the employment ladder.

options.label: D
options.text: All pay should increase each year at the same rate as the cost of living.

options.label: E
options.text: Every worker should be paid at least a living wage by those who profit from their work.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument in the paragraph is that it is wrong for the companies to be
paying their workers below a living wage and expecting the government to
subsidise the difference. The principle behind this statement is that companies
should be paying their employees enough to live on and the government should
not be paying the difference. The main principle however relates to the living wage
so the answer is therefore E.
Let us look at why the other answers are wrong:

items.text:
A- This statement is false and not supported by the text- it is the companies that
are leaving holes in millions of paycheques
items.label: A

items.text:

incomes because of companies
items.label: B

items.text:
C- This is true but simply restates part of the paragraph- it is not the underlying
principle
items.label: C

items.text:
D- While this is true and in some sense relates to the underlying principle, it
makes no mention of the companies which should be paying the living wage
items.label: D

In particular, many people cite a poor relationship with their boss as a reason for leaving. Typically, they’ll go to another job and find another difficult boss and the process continues. We put the responsibility for knowing our expectations onto the difficult person and then blame them when they disappoint us. Their leading officials are appointed by the government and these appointments are always the result of political power games. Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

When it comes to genius, the only possibilities are that it is something innate in people, or it is something to do with their upbringing. It is hard to imagine how simply bringing someone up in a certain way would be enough to turn them into a Mozart or a Shakespeare or an Einstein.

question_view.question_text:
The population pyramid below shows the age and gender distribution of the residents in England and Wales in 2010.
Which one of the following statements is not true?

main_body.text: The population pyramid below shows the age and gender distribution of the residents in England and Wales in 2010.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following statements is not true?

options.label: A
options.text: Over the age of 34, the number of women is higher than that of men for every age group.

options.label: B
options.text: Below the age of 35, the number of men is higher than that of women in every age group.

options.label: C
options.text: There are more than twice as many women as men in the 85+ age group.

options.label: D
options.text:
Not taking children below the age of 1 into consideration, the least numerous age group is
that of people aged 80 to 84.

options.label: E
options.text: The most numerous age group consists of people aged between 40 and 44.

question_view.question_text:
Many people criticise what they call ‘the younger generation’ for what their seniors regard as immoral behaviour. These critics need to realise that because the world has changed, moral standards have changed with it. In fact, technology is advancing so rapidly that it is only the young who understand the world in which they live. It is they, not their parents or grandparents, who should be setting moral standards. Anyone over the age of 25 cannot help but be blinded by what they learned in the past. Their education has prevented them from perceiving and responding to the demands of the modern day, and so their moral judgments have no validity.
Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

main_body.text: Many people criticise what they call ‘the younger generation’ for what their seniors regard as immoral behaviour. These critics need to realise that because the world has changed, moral standards have changed with it. In fact, technology is advancing so rapidly that it is only the young who understand the world in which they live. It is they, not their parents or grandparents, who should be setting moral standards. Anyone over the age of 25 cannot help but be blinded by what they learned in the past. Their education has prevented them from perceiving and responding to the demands of the modern day, and so their moral judgments have no validity.

options.text: Moral judgments made by people over the age of 25 are not valid.

options.label: B
options.text: Moral standards have changed.

options.label: C
options.text: Moral standards should be set by people under the age of 25.

options.label: D
options.text: The younger generation is guilty of what older people regard as immoral behaviour.

options.label: E
options.text: Young people are the only ones who understand the contemporary world.

blocks.text:
The main argument of this paragraph is that with the advent of technology,
only young people are fully equipped to understand the challenges of the day. They
are therefore uniquely poised to set the moral standard that we should live by and
this is the conclusion of the passage. The answer is therefore C.
Let us look at why the other answer choices are wrong:

items.text:
A- Although this can be inferred by the passage, it is not the conclusion. This is
the reason why only young people should set standards
items.label: A

items.text:
B- This is true and again is the reason that young people should set moral
standards
items.label: B

items.text: D- This is an example of how the older generation’s standards are no longer valid
items.label: D

items.text:
E- This again is a reason for them to set the moral standards and not a
conclusion of the passage
items.label: E

blocks.text:
We are simply required to find the “phase” (location of moon within period) of
each moon at these time intervals and see which has all three moons at the same
phase. To get the phase at a certain time, we divide the time by the period. This
means that one period (corresponding to a phase of 360 degrees/2*pi radians) has
a phase of 1. We only need to consider the phase within a cycle so we can ignore
the number before the decimal point. For example, to get the phase of a orbit with
period 20 days after 54 day, we first remove any whole periods: 54-20-20=14. This
corresponds to ignoring the part before the decimal point. After this we divide by
the period to get a phase of 14/20.

We will simply use a decimal number for the phase as the units do not actually
matter:

items.text: Every 36 days: Othello=16/20, Hamlet=36/45 and Romeo=36/120
Every 72 days: Othello=12/20, Hamlet=37/45 and Romeo=72/120
Every 132 days: Othello=12/20, Hamlet=42/45 and Romeo= 12/120
Every 180 days: Othello=0, Hamlet=0 and Romeo=½
Every 216 days: Othello=16/20, Hamlet=36/45 and Romeo=96/120

blocks.text:
The only answer with all three moons at the same phase (hence will appear
collinear) is answer choice E

A café owner makes 50 mini pizzas and 50 flapjacks for sale during the day. The pizzas are sold for $2.00 each and the flapjacks are sold for $1.00 each. However, by the end of lunchtime there are 10 mini pizzas still unsold and 15 flapjacks unsold, so the price of each is halved for the afternoon. At the end of the day there are still 2 mini pizzas and 1 flapjack left which are given away free to the last customer.
If the original 50 mini pizzas and 50 flapjacks had a combined production cost of $30.00, how much profit is made on the sale of the mini pizzas and flapjacks for the day?

However, by the end of lunchtime there are 10 mini pizzas still unsold and 15 flapjacks unsold, so the price of each is halved for the afternoon. The decline in voter turnout at elections is chiefly explained by the decline in voting by younger people. Older people are much more likely to vote. If this trend continues, we will reach a point at which no government can be said to have a mandate to govern as the number of voters will be too small to indicate the wishes of the majority. We need, therefore, to find an alternative to conventional elections so that the wishes of the people can be heard.
Which one of the following best expresses the flaw in the above argument?

If this trend continues, we will reach a point at which no government can be said to have a mandate to govern as the number of voters will be too small to indicate the wishes of the majority. We need, therefore, to find an alternative to conventional elections so that the wishes of the people can be heard.

options.text: There may be problems in using alternatives such as internet and postal voting.

options.label: B
options.text: Young people may be more likely to join a pressure group than to vote in an election.

options.text: All European countries have seen a decline in voter turnout.

options.label: D

If this happens, the current age-related difference does not necessarily indicate a continuing decline in turnout. The argument therefore fails to distinguish a persistent generational trend from behaviour that changes with age.

items.text: Declining turnout in European countries would provide evidence about the geographical extent of the trend but would not establish that it must continue indefinitely.

But this has been unfair to other workers in the company, some of whom were probably more talented and experienced than the boss’s son. There is then a tendency not to change banks: eleven per cent of bank customers are still with the bank their parents set them up with when they were a child and haven’t changed it since. Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

main_body.text: In the UK, most people open a bank account in their teenage years. There is then a tendency not to change banks: eleven per cent of bank customers are still with the bank their parents set them up with when they were a child and haven’t changed it since. This strongly suggests that, contrary to what most commentators say, people are not unhappy with the service that their banks provide.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Nearly two-thirds of UK bank customers have changed banks and two per cent have switched over five times.

options.label: B
options.text: Bank customers say that they feel that all banks provide the same level of service.

options.label: C
options.text: Nearly two-thirds of customers say they are happy with their bank’s service.

options.label: D
options.text: Bank services change as people get older and their needs change.

options.text: It is not difficult to change banks.

blocks.text: The argument infers general satisfaction with banking services from customers' tendency to remain with their existing banks, particularly the 11% who still use their childhood bank. However, A states that nearly two-thirds of customers have actually changed banks, with some switching repeatedly. This substantially limits how far the behaviour of the 11% can support a conclusion about customers generally. Although switching does not necessarily prove dissatisfaction, evidence that a much larger proportion have switched undermines the reliance on customer loyalty as an indication of widespread satisfaction. Therefore, A most weakens the argument.

items.label: B
items.text: Believing all banks offer similar services could explain why dissatisfied customers might remain with their current bank. However, this belief does not establish actual dissatisfaction or its prevalence, making it a less direct challenge than the widespread switching in A.

items.text: Nearly two-thirds explicitly reporting satisfaction would directly support the conclusion that customers are generally happy with their banking services.

items.label: D
items.text: Changing financial needs could explain some decisions to switch banks, but it does not establish that customers who remain are dissatisfied.

items.label: E
items.text: If changing banks is easy, remaining with an existing bank may be a more meaningful voluntary choice. This does not weaken the suggested connection between loyalty and satisfaction.

Surely if someone is really keen to stay fit they go jogging rather than join a health club? The health club phenomenon is just an example of how easily people can be swayed by marketing. They pay to jog on the spot when they could jog around the park for free. The vast majority of members barely use their health clubs and feel they are achieving something just by paying the fees.

Tasty Crisps are currently running a promotion in which there is one money-off coupon inside every packet. Some coupons are worth 19p, some are worth 12p and others are worth 7p.
My friend tells me that he has at least one of each value and his seven coupons have a total value of exactly £1.
How many of my friend’s coupons are worth 19p?

main_body.text:
Tasty Crisps are currently running a promotion in which there is one money-off coupon inside every packet. Some coupons are worth 19p, some are worth 12p and others are worth 7p.
My friend tells me that he has at least one of each value and his seven coupons have a total value of exactly £1.

question_view.main_question: How many of my friend’s coupons are worth 19p?

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text: Let x, y and z represent the numbers of 19p, 12p and 7p coupons. There are seven coupons worth 100p altogether, so x + y + z = 7 and 19x + 12y + 7z = 100. Substituting z = 7 − x − y gives 12x + 5y = 51. Since 5y is divisible by 5, 12x must leave a remainder of 1 when divided by 5. With at least one coupon of each value, x must be between 1 and 5. The only possible value is x = 3. Then y = 3 and z = 1, giving 3(19) + 3(12) + 1(7) = 100p. Therefore, C is correct: three coupons are worth 19p.

items.text: If x = 1, the equation requires y = 39/5 = 7.8, which cannot represent a whole number of coupons.

items.label: B
items.text: If x = 2, the equation requires y = 27/5 = 5.4, again violating the requirement for whole coupons.

items.label: D
items.text: If x = 4, the equation requires y = 3/5 = 0.6, which is not a valid coupon count.

items.label: E
items.text: If x = 5, then 12x = 60, already greater than the required total of 51 before including any 12p coupons.

Increasing attention is being paid to the environmental consequences of the plastic ‘single-use’ shopping bags provided to customers by supermarkets and other retailers. Not only does the production of these bags represent a wasteful use of natural resources, but there are also problems surrounding their disposal. For instance, the bags often end up as litter, and in the marine environment, they kill many animals that become entangled in them or mistake them for food. Numerous countries and individual cities have banned these bags, but experts on the environmental impacts of products warn that no perfect alternative exists. Whether using fabric or heavier plastic, manufacturing bags that are stronger and thus more reusable requires significantly greater quantities of natural resources than the vilified ‘single-use’ ones.
Which one of the following is a conclusion that can be drawn from the above passage?

main_body.text: Increasing attention is being paid to the environmental consequences of the plastic ‘single-use’ shopping bags provided to customers by supermarkets and other retailers. Not only does the production of these bags represent a wasteful use of natural resources, but there are also problems surrounding their disposal. For instance, the bags often end up as litter, and in the marine environment, they kill many animals that become entangled in them or mistake them for food. Numerous countries and individual cities have banned these bags, but experts on the environmental impacts of products warn that no perfect alternative exists. Whether using fabric or heavier plastic, manufacturing bags that are stronger and thus more reusable requires significantly greater quantities of natural resources than the vilified ‘single-use’ ones.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is a conclusion that can be drawn from the above passage?

options.text: Encouraging consumers to change their behaviour is not an effective solution to environmental problems.

options.label: B
options.text: Product bans are never an effective solution to environmental problems.

options.label: C
options.text: The solution to environmental problems lies in limiting human population growth.

options.label: D
options.text: Recycled paper bags should be used instead of plastic bags.

options.label: E
options.text: When comparing two products from an environmental standpoint, it is important to consider their manufacturing processes, length of use, and disposal.

blocks.text: Single-use plastic bags create environmental problems through resource consumption during manufacturing and harmful consequences after disposal. However, stronger reusable alternatives require more natural resources to manufacture. Therefore, an environmental comparison cannot consider production or disposal in isolation. It must also account for how long each product is used, since reusability affects how manufacturing costs should be evaluated. This supports E: manufacturing processes, length of use and disposal must all be considered when comparing products environmentally.

items.label: A
items.text: The passage does not establish that changing consumer behaviour is ineffective. Reusing bags is itself a behavioural consideration relevant to their environmental impact.

items.label: B
items.text: The existence of disadvantages in alternatives to plastic bags does not prove that product bans are never effective. This is an unsupported absolute generalisation.

items.label: C
items.text: The passage examines the environmental consequences of shopping bags, not population growth. It provides no basis for identifying population restrictions as the solution.

items.label: D
items.text: The passage does not establish that recycled paper bags have lower overall environmental costs than plastic bags. Their manufacturing, usage and disposal impacts are not compared.

Several cities around the world have introduced congestion charging schemes. Drivers are expected to pay a fee in order to drive inside the charging zone. In recent years, some schemes have offered discounts or entirely waived the charge for vehicles that cause less pollution. This is, however, an illogical and unfair policy that should not continue. Congestion is unaffected by emissions, and those cars that have low emissions still contribute to congestion.
Those who cannot afford to buy a low-emission car are still expected to pay the charge even if the roads they drive on remain congested.
Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

main_body.text:
Several cities around the world have introduced congestion charging schemes. Drivers are expected to pay a fee in order to drive inside the charging zone. In recent years, some schemes have offered discounts or entirely waived the charge for vehicles that cause less pollution. This is, however, an illogical and unfair policy that should not continue. Congestion is unaffected by emissions, and those cars that have low emissions still contribute to congestion.
Those who cannot afford to buy a low-emission car are still expected to pay the charge even if the roads they drive on remain congested.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The principal purpose of a congestion charge is to reduce congestion.

options.label: B
options.text: It is not important to try to reduce car emissions in cities.

options.label: C
options.text: All drivers would buy low-emission vehicles if they could afford to do so.

options.label: D
options.text: Congestion charging has not had any positive effects where it has been used.

options.label: E
options.text: If everyone drove low-emission cars, nobody would have to pay the charges.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text: The argument opposes discounts for low-emission vehicles because those vehicles still contribute to traffic congestion. This criticism depends on treating congestion reduction as the principal objective of congestion charging. If reducing pollution were instead the primary purpose, discounting cleaner vehicles could be reasonable even though they contribute equally to congestion. Therefore, the argument requires A: the principal purpose of a congestion charge is to reduce congestion. Without this assumption, the fact that cleaner vehicles still cause congestion would not establish that emission-based discounts are inappropriate.

items.label: B
items.text: The argument does not require emissions reduction to be unimportant. It only requires congestion reduction to be the principal objective when evaluating congestion-charge discounts.

items.label: C
items.text: Whether all drivers would purchase low-emission vehicles if they could afford them does not determine whether cleaner vehicles should receive congestion-charge discounts.

items.label: D
items.text: The argument can criticise emission-based discounts even if congestion charging has produced other positive effects. Complete failure of the schemes is not a necessary assumption.

items.label: E
items.text: The passage states that some schemes offer discounts while others waive charges. It does not require the assumption that universal ownership of low-emission cars would eliminate all payments.

question_view.question_text:
We live in an information-rich world where communication is quicker and easier than ever before. We don’t have to wait for journalists and photographers to report news to us. Anyone can talk about or take photographs of significant events and share them immediately.
Traditional ways of reporting meant that news could be effectively censored, but this is no longer the case. Similarly, incorrect information cannot be removed from the public domain without great difficulty. Governments and the traditional media will therefore need to find new ways to cope with these challenges and adapt to new technology.
Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?

main_body.text:
We live in an information-rich world where communication is quicker and easier than ever before. We don’t have to wait for journalists and photographers to report news to us. Anyone can talk about or take photographs of significant events and share them immediately.
Traditional ways of reporting meant that news could be effectively censored, but this is no longer the case. Similarly, incorrect information cannot be removed from the public domain without great difficulty. Governments and the traditional media will therefore need to find new ways to cope with these challenges and adapt to new technology.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Some governments have successfully restricted the information available on the internet in their countries.

options.label: B
options.text: Journalists occasionally film material on their mobile phones.

options.label: C
options.text: Information can be posted anonymously on the internet, thus avoiding possible prosecution.

options.label: D
options.text: Legal proceedings have been brought against those publishing false and incriminating material on the internet.

options.label: E
options.text: In the past, individuals often took photographs that they then sold to the press.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text: The argument claims that modern communication technology allows information to spread rapidly and makes censorship or removal increasingly difficult. Consequently, governments and traditional media must develop new ways of responding to these challenges. C strengthens this reasoning because anonymous publication makes it harder to identify and prosecute those responsible for distributing information. This creates an additional obstacle to controlling online material, reinforcing the conclusion that established approaches must adapt.

question_view.main_question: How many tins of paint do I need to buy?

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text: The room requires painting on four walls and the ceiling, excluding the door and windows. Wall area = 2(8 × 3) + 2(4 × 3) = 72 m². Ceiling area = 8 × 4 = 32 m². Subtracting the 10 m² occupied by the door and windows gives 72 + 32 − 10 = 94 m². Each litre covers 12 m², so the required paint is 94 ÷ 12 ≈ 7.83 litres. One 8-litre tin covers 96 m², which is sufficient. Therefore, A is correct: one tin.

items.text: Two tins contain 16 litres, whereas the calculated requirement is less than 8 litres.

items.label: C
items.text: Six tins provide 48 litres, far beyond the amount required to cover the 94 m² paintable area.

items.label: D
items.text: Eight tins would cover 768 m², substantially exceeding the area requiring paint.

items.label: E
items.text: Seventeen tins provide 136 litres, sufficient to cover 1,632 m², greatly exceeding the calculated requirement.

question_view.question_text:
Anyone who lends money to anyone else without a licence is committing an offence under UK law. Some unlicensed money lenders charge excessive rates of interest, and many use threats and violence to enforce payment. It is important to protect poor and vulnerable people from being exploited in this way. So anyone convicted of this offence should be sent to prison.
Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

main_body.text: Anyone who lends money to anyone else without a licence is committing an offence under UK law. Some unlicensed money lenders charge excessive rates of interest, and many use threats and violence to enforce payment. It is important to protect poor and vulnerable people from being exploited in this way. So anyone convicted of this offence should be sent to prison.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: It appeals to the reader’s emotions by describing some people as ‘poor and vulnerable’.

options.label: B
options.text: It draws a conclusion about all unlicensed money lenders on the basis of evidence about some of them.

options.label: C
options.text: It makes a personal attack on the unlicensed money lenders.

options.label: D
options.text: It restricts the options between licensed and unlicensed money lenders.

options.label: E
options.text: It wrongly assumes that licensed money lenders do not charge excessive rates of interest.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text: The argument states that some unlicensed money lenders charge excessive interest and many use threats or violence. However, it concludes that anyone convicted of lending money without a licence should be imprisoned. This extends evidence about the harmful behaviour of some offenders to every person committing the offence, without establishing that all unlicensed lenders engage in such exploitation or deserve imprisonment. Therefore, B identifies the flaw: an unjustified generalisation from some members of a group to the entire group.

items.label: A
items.text: Describing people as poor and vulnerable may evoke sympathy, but the argument's decisive problem is that evidence about some offenders is used to justify punishing all offenders.

items.label: C
items.text: The passage criticises specific lending practices rather than attacking lenders' personal characteristics to discredit their arguments. Its conclusion concerns punishment, not the credibility of an opponent.

items.label: D
items.text: The argument concerns whether unlicensed lenders should receive prison sentences. It does not present licensed and unlicensed lending as the only available options in a decision.

items.label: E
items.text: The argument makes no claim about the interest rates charged by licensed lenders. Its proposed punishment does not depend on assuming that licensed lenders never charge excessive interest.

question_view.question_text:
Either young people are getting cleverer each year or examinations are becoming easier for students to pass. Since there is very little evidence from IQ testing and other supposed benchmarks that young people are more intelligent now than in the past, we must conclude that the examination system is easier for students today than it was in the past.
Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

main_body.text: Either young people are getting cleverer each year or examinations are becoming easier for students to pass. Since there is very little evidence from IQ testing and other supposed benchmarks that young people are more intelligent now than in the past, we must conclude that the examination system is easier for students today than it was in the past.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text:
Farmers must choose between using organic or non-organic fertilisers on their land.
Organic fertilisers can produce a lower crop yield and farmers may find it difficult to change to organic methods if they have been using non-organic methods for some time. Farmers should therefore consider the longer-term impacts of their decisions.

options.label: B
options.text: Every year millions of holidaymakers decide whether to holiday in the UK or abroad. Since most of us like to have a degree of predictability in terms of holiday weather, we should not be surprised that, given the choice, most people would holiday abroad.

options.label: C
options.text: Researchers have looked at the communication between different animals and found that meerkats have a series of alerts and calls that fall into two categories, greetings and alarms. Since we can be sure that this meerkat is not calling as a greeting, we must accept that he is attempting to raise the alarm.

options.label: D
options.text:
Wood burning stoves are a better way to heat your home than an open fire. Wood burning stoves are highly efficient, whereas an open fire loses a great deal of heat up the chimney.
More people should therefore install wood burning stoves in their homes.

options.label: E
options.text: When allocating emergency appointments, receptionists prioritise children and the elderly above other patients. If you are neither a child nor elderly, you may have to wait longer to see a doctor.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text: The original argument presents two alternatives: either students are becoming more intelligent or examinations are becoming easier. It then dismisses the first explanation because of the lack of supporting evidence and concludes that the second must be true. C follows the same structure: meerkat calls are classified as either greetings or alarms; the call is not a greeting, so it must be an alarm. Both arguments reach a conclusion by presenting two alternatives and eliminating one. The original argument's dismissal is less conclusive because a lack of evidence is not definitive disproof, but C most closely parallels its reasoning.

items.label: A
items.text: Although organic and non-organic fertilisers are presented as alternatives, neither is eliminated. The conclusion instead recommends considering long-term consequences.

items.label: B
items.text: The argument predicts a preference for holidays abroad based on desired weather predictability. It does not rule out holidays in the UK and infer the remaining alternative by elimination.

items.label: D
items.text: The argument recommends wood-burning stoves because of their greater efficiency. It relies on a comparison of advantages rather than excluding one of two possibilities.

items.label: E
items.text: The argument describes how prioritising certain patients may affect waiting times. It applies a scheduling rule rather than eliminating one alternative to establish another.

Each baby born in the UK will, during his or her lifetime, burn carbon roughly equivalent to 2½ acres of woodland – an area the size of Trafalgar Square. The UK population, now 62 million, will exceed 70 million by
2028. On average, women born outside the UK have 2.5 children compared with 1.7 for those
born in the UK. The global population of 7 billion is expected to rise to 9.2 billion by 2050.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?

blocks.text: The argument provides evidence that television has reduced family communication: families increasingly watch programmes instead of discussing things together. items.label: E

We need to change science lessons so that they give children a correct view of modern science. Children are often taught in science lessons that matter can exist in three different states – solid, liquid and gas. However, developments in science suggest that this is far too simple a picture. Government advice on alcohol drinking limits is based on studies carried out twenty-five years ago. It has often been expressed in terms of a maximum number of units per day. But advising people about a daily rate implies that drinking alcohol every day is acceptable, when up-to-date research suggests that the body needs more ‘recovery time’ than one day. Health promotion advice should avoid being so simple that it inadvertently encourages unhealthy behaviour.
Better to have more complex messages than simple messages which promote unhealthy behaviour.
Which one of the following is an assumption underlying the above argument?

main_body.text:
Government advice on alcohol drinking limits is based on studies carried out twenty-five years ago. It has often been expressed in terms of a maximum number of units per day. But advising people about a daily rate implies that drinking alcohol every day is acceptable, when up-to-date research suggests that the body needs more ‘recovery time’ than one day. Health promotion advice should avoid being so simple that it inadvertently encourages unhealthy behaviour.
Better to have more complex messages than simple messages which promote unhealthy behaviour.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is an assumption underlying the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The research carried out twenty-five years ago is no longer valid.

options.label: B
options.text: Drinking alcohol every day is common practice.

options.label: C
options.text: People always follow the advice of health promotion messages.

options.label: D
options.text: The government should regularly revise its advice on all health issues.

options.label: E
options.text: Complex health promotion messages will be read and understood.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text: The argument criticises simple daily alcohol limits because they may imply that drinking every day is acceptable, despite research suggesting that the body needs longer recovery periods. It therefore recommends using more complex health messages rather than simple ones that encourage unhealthy behaviour. However, this recommendation depends on complex messages being accessible to their intended audience. If people neither read nor understand them, greater complexity would not communicate the healthier guidance. Therefore, E expresses the required assumption that complex health promotion messages will be read and understood.

items.label: A
items.text: The argument does not require all research from twenty-five years ago to be invalid. It only requires newer findings to reveal an important limitation in existing daily drinking advice.

items.label: B
items.text: The argument concerns what daily drinking advice implies and might encourage. Drinking every day need not already be common for such advice to create a misleading impression.

items.label: C
items.text: The argument does not require everyone always to follow health advice. It only relies on messages having some influence on understanding or behaviour.

items.label: D
items.text: The argument recommends improving a particular type of health message. It does not depend on a general requirement to regularly revise government advice on every health issue.

question_view.question_text:
Studies of fossilised remains indicate that, every 20 to 30 million years, life on Earth experiences a sudden and mass extinction of all or most of its dominant species. Yet, in each case, within some 5 to 10 million years the diversity of species on the planet is as great, if not greater, than it had been previously, since the demise of the dominant species allows more minority species to flourish. Whatever disasters we may wreak on the planet, life in the long term will not only survive but actually increase in richness and diversity.
Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

main_body.text: Studies of fossilised remains indicate that, every 20 to 30 million years, life on Earth experiences a sudden and mass extinction of all or most of its dominant species. Yet, in each case, within some 5 to 10 million years the diversity of species on the planet is as great, if not greater, than it had been previously, since the demise of the dominant species allows more minority species to flourish. Whatever disasters we may wreak on the planet, life in the long term will not only survive but actually increase in richness and diversity.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The consequences of a global nuclear holocaust are not known.

options.label: B
options.text: It can be difficult to draw precise conclusions about dates from fossil records.

options.label: C
options.text: Human technology will soon be advanced enough to prevent most natural catastrophes.

options.label: D
options.text: Some species are able to withstand the most extreme forms of environmental change.

options.label: E
options.text: Some species have died out due to dramatic changes in climate.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text: The argument uses evidence of past mass extinctions followed by recoveries in biodiversity to conclude that life will survive and become more diverse regardless of any disasters humanity causes. However, A states that the consequences of a global nuclear holocaust are unknown. Such a disaster might have consequences unlike those documented in the fossil record, so past recoveries cannot establish that life would necessarily recover from it. This challenges the argument's unrestricted prediction about all possible human-caused disasters, making A the strongest weakening statement.

items.label: B
items.text: Uncertainty about precise fossil dates could affect the proposed timing of extinction cycles, but it does not directly challenge the evidence that biodiversity recovered after previous extinctions.

items.label: C
items.text: Technology preventing natural catastrophes would reduce the likelihood of certain disasters. It does not establish whether life could recover from severe human-caused destruction.

items.label: D
items.text: The ability of some species to survive extreme environmental changes supports the possibility that life could persist after disasters, although it does not guarantee increased biodiversity.

items.label: E
items.text: The extinction of some species following dramatic climate changes is compatible with the passage's description of mass extinctions. It does not challenge the claim that biodiversity subsequently recovered.

blocks.text:
The daily saving is the difference between the cost of 2 wet-food sachets and 25g of dry food from each supplier. At the pet shop, each sachet costs £12 ÷ 12 = £1, while dry food costs £4 ÷ 400 = £0.01 per gram. Daily cost = 2(£1) + 25(£0.01) = £2.25.

Online, each sachet costs £62.40 ÷ 96 = £0.65, and dry food costs £16 ÷ 2000 = £0.008 per gram. Daily cost = 2(£0.65) + 25(£0.008) = £1.50. Saving = £2.25 − £1.50 = £0.75, or 75p. Therefore, B is correct.

Arps and Urps have tails, while Orps do not. Since Billy captured 45 creatures with 33 tails, there must be 45 − 33 = 12 Orps.

options.label: A
options.text: If a house lacks both window locks and a burglar alarm, the insurance application will inevitably be turned down. Since your claim has been rejected, your house must have neither window locks nor burglar alarm.

options.label: B
options.text: If heat or light is emitted by a body, then its energy decreases. It follows that, if a body’s energy remains constant, it has emitted neither heat nor light.

options.label: C
options.text:
Anybody over 21 who holds a university degree or equivalent is eligible for selection. Since

blocks.text:

This uses the logical structure: if A or B occurs, then C follows; if C does not occur, neither A nor B can occur.

Each word in a word game is scored by adding up the values of its letters. Each letter has the same value whenever it appears but different letters have different values. I know the word values for TEAR, RITE, TREE and RAT, but none of the letter values.
How many of the letter values can I now calculate?

main_body.text: Each word in a word game is scored by adding up the values of its letters. Each letter has the same value whenever it appears but different letters have different values. I know the word values for TEAR, RITE, TREE and RAT, but none of the letter values.

question_view.main_question: How many of the letter values can I now calculate?

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The four known word scores provide four equations involving five unknown letter values: T, E, A, R and I.

TEAR and RAT contain the same letters except for E, so E = TEAR − RAT.

TREE contains T + R + 2E, while RAT contains T + R + A. Since E is known, A = RAT + 2E − TREE.

RITE contains T + R + I + E, whereas TREE contains T + R + 2E. Thus I = RITE − TREE + E.

The score of RAT now determines T + R, but not T and R individually because these letters always appear together in every supplied word. Therefore, exactly three letter values—E, A and I—can be calculated. D is correct.

items.text: Zero is incorrect because subtracting RAT from TEAR directly determines the value of E.

items.label: B
items.text: One is insufficient because, after finding E, the difference between TREE and RAT also allows A to be calculated.

items.label: C
items.text: Two is insufficient because comparing RITE with TREE additionally determines I once E is known.

items.label: E
items.text: Four is unsupported because T and R always occur together. Their combined value can be found, but neither individual value can be determined uniquely.

question_view.main_question: How many more boys than girls are there in the class?

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
Let g be the number of girls and b the number of boys. Since there are 24 pupils, g + b = 24. Each girl plants 3 roses, while every 3 boys collectively plant 1 birch tree, so the total number of plants is 3g + b/3 = 24.

Multiplying the second equation by 3 gives 9g + b = 72. Subtracting g + b = 24 gives 8g = 48, so g = 6. Therefore, b = 24 − 6 = 18.

The difference is 18 − 6 = 12 pupils. Therefore, D is correct.

blocks.text:
The original mixture contains 1 part concentrate and 4 parts water, so concentrate makes up 1/5 of the 500ml bottle: 500 ÷ 5 = 100ml.

After 100ml of well-mixed squash is spilled, 400ml remains. Its concentrate content is 400 × 1/5 = 80ml. Jake then adds 100ml of pure concentrate to restore the bottle to 500ml.

The final concentrate volume is 80 + 100 = 180ml. Therefore, the concentration is (180 ÷ 500) × 100 = 36%. The correct answer is D.

items.label: C
items.text: 28% corresponds to 140ml of concentrate in a 500ml bottle, whereas the remaining mixture and refill contain 180ml.

items.label: E
items.text: 40% would require 200ml of concentrate in the final bottle, but the calculated amount is only 180ml.

question_view.question_text:
Shooting is not just positive for rural economies, but is also necessary for conservation efforts.
In various peripheral rural places in Britain, sport shooting related jobs are a mainstay of local economies, often accounting for as much as a third of the labour market. However, since humans disturbed the ecosystem by eradicating the top predators, destroying habitats and introducing non-native species, we are also now responsible for reducing further damage –
conserving – by continuous management. This means shooting overpopulated species to minimise the risks of disease and starvation, and dominant foreign species in order to conserve weaker native ones. Additionally, the management of the environment for the purposes of sport shooting can have very positive conservation effects; for example, many endangered birds of prey now thrive on shooting estates.
Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

main_body.text:
Shooting is not just positive for rural economies, but is also necessary for conservation efforts.
In various peripheral rural places in Britain, sport shooting related jobs are a mainstay of local economies, often accounting for as much as a third of the labour market. However, since humans disturbed the ecosystem by eradicating the top predators, destroying habitats and introducing non-native species, we are also now responsible for reducing further damage –
conserving – by continuous management. This means shooting overpopulated species to minimise the risks of disease and starvation, and dominant foreign species in order to conserve weaker native ones. Additionally, the management of the environment for the purposes of sport shooting can have very positive conservation effects; for example, many endangered birds of prey now thrive on shooting estates.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Wild flower numbers and bee populations have increased on shooting estates.

options.label: B
options.text: Many animals that are shot are sold on to butchers and enter the food market.

options.label: C
options.text: People from all over the world travel to Britain to engage in sport shooting.

options.label: D
options.text: Many native species such as the red squirrel are at threat from foreign species.

options.label: E
options.text: Re-introducing top predators such as wolves is a more effective means of conservation.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument maintains that shooting is necessary for conservation because humans have disrupted ecosystems by eliminating predators, introducing foreign species and damaging habitats. It presents shooting overpopulated or invasive animals as a way to manage these problems.

E challenges the necessity of shooting by proposing that reintroducing top predators is a more effective conservation method. If restoring predators can control animal populations more effectively, conservation may be achieved without relying on shooting as the necessary solution. This directly weakens the argument's claim of necessity, although it does not dispute shooting's possible economic benefits.

items.label: A
items.text: Increased wildflowers and bee populations on shooting estates would provide additional evidence that the management of these estates can benefit conservation.

items.label: B
items.text: Selling shot animals for food describes another use of the animals but does not establish that shooting is unnecessary or ineffective for conservation.

items.label: C
items.text: International visitors participating in sport shooting could contribute to rural economies, supporting the economic part of the argument rather than undermining its conservation claims.

items.label: D
items.text: Threats to native species from introduced foreign species support the argument's concern that such species require management to protect native populations.

question_view.question_text:
Thousands of parents have recently been prosecuted by local education authorities for taking their children out of school to go on holiday during term time. I took my daughter out of primary school for a two-week holiday every year. The headmistress made no objection and said it would give the other kids time to catch up with her! She was able to learn a foreign language and spend some rewarding time with her French pen-pal. She eventually achieved top grades at school and a degree in mathematics, so it obviously did her no harm! Parents, not governments, know best how to raise children. This law is quite unnecessary.
Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

main_body.text: Thousands of parents have recently been prosecuted by local education authorities for taking their children out of school to go on holiday during term time. I took my daughter out of primary school for a two-week holiday every year. The headmistress made no objection and said it would give the other kids time to catch up with her! She was able to learn a foreign language and spend some rewarding time with her French pen-pal. She eventually achieved top grades at school and a degree in mathematics, so it obviously did her no harm! Parents, not governments, know best how to raise children. This law is quite unnecessary.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: It is an appeal to tradition because it suggests that taking children on holiday in term time used to be acceptable.

options.label: B
options.text: It is based on authority as it uses the headmistress’s lack of objection in support.

options.label: C
options.text: It assumes that because the daughter’s good grades were achieved after her foreign holidays, they were the result of the holidays.

options.label: D
options.text: It is based entirely on the one example of the daughter and generalises from that.

options.label: E
options.text: It assumes that learning some French adequately compensated for the work the daughter missed.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The author argues that laws restricting term-time holidays are unnecessary, using the experience of one daughter who missed school for holidays yet subsequently achieved excellent academic results. However, the fact that one child experienced no apparent educational harm does not establish that term-time absences are harmless for children generally.

Different children may have different learning needs and may be affected differently by missing lessons. The argument therefore generalises from one favourable personal example to a broad policy conclusion. This is the flaw identified by D.

items.label: A
items.text: The author mentions past experience but does not claim that term-time holidays should be permitted simply because they were previously acceptable. The argument relies on the daughter's outcome.

items.label: B
items.text: The headmistress's approval supports the description of the individual case, but the wider conclusion is based primarily on the daughter's success rather than the headmistress's authority.

items.label: C
items.text: The author uses the daughter's good grades to suggest the holidays did not harm her education. The argument does not need to claim that the holidays caused those grades.

items.label: E
items.text: Learning French is presented as one benefit of the holidays, but the author also cites subsequent academic success. The conclusion does not depend specifically on French learning compensating for missed schoolwork.

question_view.question_text:
Evidence suggests that children whose parents are married tend to fare better – financially, academically and socially – than children of unmarried parents. The government is therefore proposing a tax break for married couples, whereby married couples are reimbursed by approximately £150 per person per annum. This idea is flawed for several reasons. First, it punishes those whose partners have left them and broken up the marriage. Secondly, it punishes those who, through no fault of their own, have been unable to find a partner. Thirdly, it assumes that people in unhappy relationships will persevere in their unhappy state for something like £12.50 a month. This is patently absurd. Finally, it makes the bogus assumption that maintaining a poor marriage will be better for the children than separation.
Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

main_body.text: Evidence suggests that children whose parents are married tend to fare better – financially, academically and socially – than children of unmarried parents. The government is therefore proposing a tax break for married couples, whereby married couples are reimbursed by approximately £150 per person per annum. This idea is flawed for several reasons. First, it punishes those whose partners have left them and broken up the marriage. Secondly, it punishes those who, through no fault of their own, have been unable to find a partner. Thirdly, it assumes that people in unhappy relationships will persevere in their unhappy state for something like £12.50 a month. This is patently absurd. Finally, it makes the bogus assumption that maintaining a poor marriage will be better for the children than separation.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: A poor relationship could be more damaging for a child than separation.

options.label: B
options.text: Children whose parents are married tend to fare better than children of unmarried parties.

options.label: C
options.text: It is absurd to think that people will persevere in an unhappy relationship for the sum proposed.

options.label: D
options.text: The government’s proposal punishes single parents.

options.label: E
options.text: The government’s idea of giving married couples tax breaks is flawed.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The passage argues against the government's proposal to provide tax breaks to married couples. Although evidence suggests that children of married parents tend to fare better, the author identifies several problems with using financial incentives to encourage marriage: disadvantages for people whose relationships ended or who cannot find partners, the limited financial incentive for unhappy couples, and the unsupported assumption that remaining in an unhappy marriage benefits children.

These criticisms all support the overall judgement that the proposed tax-break policy is flawed. Therefore, E expresses the main conclusion.

items.label: A
items.text: The possibility that an unhappy relationship harms children is one reason used to criticise the policy, not the author's overall conclusion about the tax break.

items.label: B
items.text: The tendency for children of married parents to fare better is introduced as evidence motivating the government's proposal. It is not the conclusion the author seeks to establish.

items.label: C
items.text: The inadequacy of the financial incentive for unhappy couples is one supporting criticism, not the complete argument against the policy.

items.label: D
items.text: The policy's disadvantage to some single people is another reason for opposing it, but the argument also raises concerns about incentives and children's welfare.

The award of a Nobel Prize in economics, but not in psychology, sociology or anthropology, seems to imply that economics is not a social science, but an exact one, like chemistry or physics. Underpinning this idea is the thought that the human world operates like the physical world. Economists themselves perpetuate this impression by dealing in hard quantitative data, as opposed to observation and qualitative analysis. The defining feature of the natural sciences is their consistent success in making predictions, but almost all economists failed to predict the
2008 financial crisis. The striking collapse of LTCM, a hedge fund set up by two economists who were later awarded the Nobel Prize, further underscores the limits of economics to make accurate forecasts.
Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?

main_body.text:
The award of a Nobel Prize in economics, but not in psychology, sociology or anthropology, seems to imply that economics is not a social science, but an exact one, like chemistry or physics. Underpinning this idea is the thought that the human world operates like the physical world. Economists themselves perpetuate this impression by dealing in hard quantitative data, as opposed to observation and qualitative analysis. The defining feature of the natural sciences is their consistent success in making predictions, but almost all economists failed to predict the
2008 financial crisis. The striking collapse of LTCM, a hedge fund set up by two economists who were later awarded the Nobel Prize, further underscores the limits of economics to make accurate forecasts.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?

options.text: The Nobel Prize should not be awarded for economics.

options.label: B
options.text: The human world is not part of the physical world.

options.label: C
options.text: Economics is not a science like chemistry or physics.

options.text: Economists cannot predict the behaviour of markets.

options.label: E
options.text: Hard quantitative data has no role in economics.

blocks.text:
The passage distinguishes economics from natural sciences by emphasising the consistent predictive success attributed to sciences such as chemistry and physics. Although economics uses quantitative data and is sometimes presented as an exact science, the author points to economists' widespread failure to predict the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of a hedge fund established by prominent economists.

These examples challenge the claim that economics possesses the same forecasting reliability as the natural sciences. Therefore, C follows: economics is not a science in the same sense as chemistry or physics, particularly regarding consistent predictive success.

items.text: The passage questions the impression created by awarding a Nobel Prize in economics, but it does not conclude that the award itself should be abolished.

items.label: B

items.label: D
items.text: The failure to predict major events demonstrates limitations in economic forecasting, not that economists are incapable of making any accurate market predictions.

items.label: E

Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

main_body.text:
Mobile phone use and driving under the influence of alcohol are not the only examples of irresponsible driver behaviour. Tiredness when driving a vehicle is said to be responsible for
300 deaths per year. Astonishingly, almost half of male drivers and 22% of female drivers admit to having fallen asleep at the wheel. If we assume (and it seems reasonable to do so) that even more people are injured than killed as a result of accidents caused by tiredness, it is clear that tiredness while driving is a major road safety issue – and entirely preventable. If we wish to preserve our own lives and those of others we should not drive a car knowing that we have had insufficient sleep or rest to drive safely.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.label: B
options.text: Drivers are able to recognise when they are dangerously tired.

options.label: C
options.text: Falling asleep when driving is more dangerous than using a mobile phone while driving.

options.label: D
options.text: People whose jobs involve long distance driving can always avoid driving while tired.

options.label: E
options.text: Tiredness has been insufficiently highlighted in road safety campaigns.

blocks.text:

If drivers cannot identify dangerous fatigue, they cannot reliably act on the instruction to avoid driving when insufficiently rested. Therefore, B is the underlying assumption linking the proposed precaution to the prevention of fatigue-related accidents.

items.text: The reported differences in falling asleep at the wheel do not establish that women are generally more careful. The argument does not require any explanation of those differences.

items.label: C

items.label: D
items.text: The argument recommends avoiding unsafe driving, but it does not require every professional long-distance driver to be able to avoid fatigue in all circumstances.

items.label: E

question_view.question_text:
There has been a significant rise in the number of children with rickets. This has resulted from the airless, indoor world we have created for ourselves. Rickets is caused by a deficiency of vitamin D, which is produced in response to sunlight on the skin. Where children used to play outside they mostly stay indoors immersed in virtual realities via various electronic media. Instead of long summer evenings outdoors, we close the curtains to prevent sunlight falling on our screens. The lure of technology is compounded by adult fears of the risks to children if they are left to roam free in the outside world; in any case there are fewer accessible public spaces for open air activity. Curing this will require an awful lot more than vitamin pills.
Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

main_body.text: There has been a significant rise in the number of children with rickets. This has resulted from the airless, indoor world we have created for ourselves. Rickets is caused by a deficiency of vitamin D, which is produced in response to sunlight on the skin. Where children used to play outside they mostly stay indoors immersed in virtual realities via various electronic media. Instead of long summer evenings outdoors, we close the curtains to prevent sunlight falling on our screens. The lure of technology is compounded by adult fears of the risks to children if they are left to roam free in the outside world; in any case there are fewer accessible public spaces for open air activity. Curing this will require an awful lot more than vitamin pills.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: There has been a large growth in areas designated as national parks and in urban parkland.

options.label: B
options.text: Diet has a much more significant effect on vitamin D intake than sunlight.

options.label: C
options.text: The incidence of rickets is confined to a few hundred cases a year.

options.label: D
options.text: In the 19th century, when the incidence of rickets was much higher, terrible air pollution and smog affected the large population of city dwellers.

options.label: E
options.text: Many people can’t afford or be relied on to take vitamin D supplements.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument attributes rising cases of rickets mainly to children spending more time indoors, where they receive less sunlight and consequently produce less vitamin D. It concludes that addressing the problem requires broader changes than simply providing vitamin supplements.

B weakens this explanation by stating that diet has a much greater influence on vitamin D intake than sunlight. If dietary factors are substantially more important, reduced outdoor activity may be less significant as the cause of vitamin D deficiency than the passage suggests. This challenges the argument's emphasis on an indoor lifestyle as the central explanation for increasing rickets cases.

items.label: A
items.text: An increase in parkland could challenge the claim that outdoor spaces are becoming less available, but it does not establish that children actually spend more time outdoors or receive enough sunlight.

items.label: C
items.text: A few hundred annual cases could still represent a significant increase from an earlier level. The absolute number does not directly challenge the proposed cause.

items.label: D

Five girls are collecting shells on a beach. They are putting them in buckets that each hold 24 shells. At the end of the collecting time, they are going to ensure that they all have the same number of shells. Four of them are only two short of filling their bucket, but the youngest one is lagging behind with her total. Each of the others give her three shells from their buckets in order to equalise the numbers collected.
How many shells did the youngest girl collect for herself?

main_body.text: Five girls are collecting shells on a beach. They are putting them in buckets that each hold 24 shells. At the end of the collecting time, they are going to ensure that they all have the same number of shells. question_view.main_question: How many shells did the youngest girl collect for herself?

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
Four girls each collected 24 − 2 = 22 shells. Each then gives 3 shells to the youngest girl, leaving each of the four with 22 − 3 = 19 shells.

To make all five totals equal, the youngest girl must also finish with 19 shells. She receives 4 × 3 = 12 shells from the others, so the number she originally collected is 19 − 12 = 7. Therefore, B is correct.

question_view.question_text:
When mobile phones first became relatively inexpensive many parents bought them for their teenage children on the grounds that having access to a phone would keep them safe. High profile cases of abduction at the time underscored the need to improve safety for young people. But today mobile phones invariably have access to the internet, which has made young people vulnerable to stalking and cyberbullying. Since the stated case for buying teenagers mobile phones was to keep them safe, we should now restrict their access to them.
Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

main_body.text: When mobile phones first became relatively inexpensive many parents bought them for their teenage children on the grounds that having access to a phone would keep them safe. High profile cases of abduction at the time underscored the need to improve safety for young people. But today mobile phones invariably have access to the internet, which has made young people vulnerable to stalking and cyberbullying. Since the stated case for buying teenagers mobile phones was to keep them safe, we should now restrict their access to them.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The incidence of cyberbullying and stalking does not undermine the respects in which mobile phones keep teenagers safe.

options.label: B
options.text: If you restrict young people’s access to mobile phones they will continue to bully one another on other devices.

options.label: C
options.text: Access to mobile phones has not stopped teenagers from being attacked while out alone at night.

options.label: D
options.text: The majority of teenagers are not affected by the problems of stalking and cyberbullying.

options.label: E
options.text: It ignores the fact that there are other ways of keeping children safe.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The original justification for giving teenagers mobile phones was that they could improve safety, particularly in situations such as abduction. The argument now recommends restricting phones because internet access exposes teenagers to stalking and cyberbullying.

However, introducing new risks does not establish that the original safety benefits have disappeared. Mobile phones could still protect teenagers in certain situations while exposing them to different dangers. The argument fails to consider both effects before recommending restrictions. Therefore, A identifies the flaw.

items.label: B
items.text: Bullying through other devices might limit the effectiveness of restricting phones, but this is a separate practical objection. The central flaw is the failure to consider the phones' continuing safety benefits.

items.label: C
items.text: The passage does not claim that phones prevent every attack. Their failure to prevent some incidents would not establish that they provide no protection in other situations.

items.label: D
items.text: Even if most teenagers were unaffected by stalking or cyberbullying, those risks could still be significant. The flaw concerns overlooking existing benefits, not the precise proportion affected.

items.label: E
items.text: Alternative ways of protecting children might exist, but the argument does not depend on phones being the only safety measure. The problem is that their original benefits are disregarded.
