main_body.text: A new supermarket scheme awards money-off vouchers to customers who spend £40 a week on their grocery shopping. As your weekly shop only costs £15, you are not eligible for vouchers.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: A discount is given to gym members who introduce new customers. You brought two friends who joined up, so you will get a discount.

options.label: B
options.text: Dessert is given to all those who have completed their main course. You have not eaten your main course so you will not be given dessert.

options.label: C
options.text:
Anyone between the ages of 18–30 inclusive gets admission into the nightclub half-price.
You are 30 so you will not pay full price.

options.label: D
options.text: A bursary is given to those on incomes below £10000. You earn £9000 so you will receive a bursary.

options.label: E
options.text: Only experienced wine drinkers can appreciate a good wine. You prefer poor quality wine as you have only recently started drinking wine.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The supermarket scheme establishes that customers spending £40 a week receive vouchers. The argument then concludes that spending only £15 means receiving no vouchers. However, the stated rule guarantees vouchers to customers meeting the threshold without explicitly ruling out vouchers for other customers.

B follows the same reasoning: completing a main course guarantees dessert, but the argument concludes that someone who has not completed it will receive no dessert. Both arguments incorrectly infer that failing a stated sufficient condition makes the outcome impossible. Therefore, B is the closest parallel.

items.label: A
items.text: Introducing new gym customers satisfies the stated condition for receiving a discount. The conclusion applies the rule directly rather than denying the benefit because the condition is absent.

items.label: C
items.text: Being 30 satisfies the stated age requirement of 18–30 inclusive. The conclusion correctly applies the eligibility rule to someone within that range.

items.label: D
items.text: An income of £9000 satisfies the stated requirement of earning below £10000. The conclusion follows from meeting the condition rather than failing it.

items.label: E
items.text: The argument treats experience as necessary for appreciating good wine, then draws a conclusion about preferring poor wine. That additional preference is not established by the condition.

question_view.question_text:
The plethora of house-buying and relocation programmes on television these days may well stimulate an interest in lovely properties, but they are a bad thing because at the same time they make viewers who could never afford the houses shown feel both envious and worthless.
Which one of the following illustrates the principle used in the above argument?

main_body.text: The plethora of house-buying and relocation programmes on television these days may well stimulate an interest in lovely properties, but they are a bad thing because at the same time they make viewers who could never afford the houses shown feel both envious and worthless.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following illustrates the principle used in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: People who watch house-buying programmes do not tend to have nice houses themselves.

options.label: B
options.text: Seeing others enjoy luxuries that they have not got can motivate people to work harder to earn enough to support the same lifestyle.

options.label: C
options.text: The public thinks a celebrity lifestyle must be great, but most celebrities are constantly worried about dropping out of the public eye.

options.label: D
options.text: It is said that renting property is throwing money away, but so much of what one pays monthly on a mortgage goes on interest anyway that many people find it better to rent rather than buy.

options.label: E
options.text: Magazines that show images of men and women who seem perfect are largely to blame for our discontent and for the increase in eating disorders among young people.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument condemns house-buying television programmes because they display attractive properties that many viewers cannot afford. Rather than merely generating interest, these programmes are claimed to create envy and feelings of worthlessness through comparison with unattainable lifestyles.

E illustrates the same principle: magazines displaying seemingly perfect people can encourage harmful comparisons with unrealistic ideals, producing dissatisfaction and potentially damaging consequences. Both arguments criticise media content for encouraging people to compare themselves unfavourably with idealised images.

items.label: A
items.text: This describes the housing circumstances of viewers but does not establish that watching attractive properties causes envy or feelings of inadequacy.

items.label: B

question_view.question_text:
Long-term unemployment is a big problem for the UK, both for the government and for the individual. The solution is unlikely to be one the government wishes to consider: invest money in improving the skills of job centre staff. Some people argue that providing welfare benefits makes unemployed people less motivated to find work. Other people, mostly outside the government, think that not enough is done to provide the help needed to get people into work.
Neither side is right. Unemployed people are all different: some really want to work and would do so if they had help; others are content to live on benefits. We have to steer away from one-
size-fits-all solutions and tailor the approach to the individual. But this needs much higher levels of skilled staff than job centres currently have.
Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

Because these differences make uniform policies inadequate, effective employment support requires individually tailored approaches. The author argues that implementing such approaches depends on having more highly skilled job-centre staff. Therefore, the principal recommendation is to invest in improving staff skills, as expressed in D.

items.label: A
items.text: Long-term unemployment is introduced as a serious problem, but the passage's main purpose is to recommend a particular solution rather than establish its relative importance.

items.label: B
items.text: Differences in motivation among unemployed people provide evidence for using tailored support. They are a supporting premise, not the policy conclusion.

items.label: C
items.text: The passage suggests tailored approaches require more skilled staff, but it does not compare their total costs with uniform approaches or claim that cheaper solutions should be preferred.

items.label: E
items.text: The possible disincentive created by welfare benefits is presented as one side of a debate that the author considers inadequate. It is not the author's main conclusion.

question_view.question_text:
A Prime Minister has a difficult judgement to make when deciding whether to sack one of their ministers or not. Faced, for example, with a minister involved in some kind of scandal, the Prime Minister might feel they should sack them to show they stand up for integrity and high moral standards, or, on the other hand, allow them to remain in post for other reasons such as loyalty to a colleague or a belief that they are, on balance, doing a good job. Sacking ministers shows that the Prime Minister is prepared to live by principles, even if by so doing they lose valued colleagues. The electorate will judge the Prime Minister to have acted with integrity: that is an invaluable perception for anyone wishing to remain in power.
Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?

main_body.text: A Prime Minister has a difficult judgement to make when deciding whether to sack one of their ministers or not. Faced, for example, with a minister involved in some kind of scandal, the Prime Minister might feel they should sack them to show they stand up for integrity and high moral standards, or, on the other hand, allow them to remain in post for other reasons such as loyalty to a colleague or a belief that they are, on balance, doing a good job. Sacking ministers shows that the Prime Minister is prepared to live by principles, even if by so doing they lose valued colleagues. The electorate will judge the Prime Minister to have acted with integrity: that is an invaluable perception for anyone wishing to remain in power.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?

options.label: A
options.text: It is in the Prime Minister’s electoral interests to err on the side of sacking.

options.label: B
options.text: Restoring public trust at a time when the reputation of politicians is low is a priority.

options.label: C
options.text: Ministers are often sacked for a relatively minor wrongdoing when this is not in the interests of the country.

options.label: D
options.text: Ministers involved in scandals should always be sacked.

options.label: E
options.text: Politicians seek to stay in power at all costs.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument states that dismissing a minister involved in a scandal demonstrates the Prime Minister's commitment to integrity and moral principles, even when the minister is personally valued or performs well. It further claims that voters will perceive such a decision as evidence of integrity, which is valuable for remaining in power.

Therefore, when the Prime Minister is uncertain whether to dismiss a minister, the electoral benefit of appearing principled provides a reason to favour dismissal. This supports A: it is in the Prime Minister's electoral interests to err on the side of sacking.

items.label: B
items.text: The passage discusses the electoral value of being perceived as principled but does not establish that politicians currently suffer from unusually low public trust.

items.label: C
items.text: No evidence is provided that ministers are frequently dismissed for minor misconduct or that such dismissals damage the country's interests.

items.label: D
items.text: The passage recognises legitimate considerations favouring retaining ministers. It supports a tendency towards dismissal, not an absolute rule requiring dismissal after every scandal.

items.label: E
items.text: The argument identifies remaining in power as an important political objective, but it does not claim politicians pursue that objective regardless of every other consideration.

question_view.question_text:
In a survey done by a school librarian during one year, borrowing of books in the library declined by 20%. Amongst books borrowed, rates of late return or loss of books also increased by 10%. On the other hand, student use of computers in the library increased by 25%. This finding was reinforced by frequent complaints from students that there were no computers available when they needed to use them. The librarian concluded that the best response to these findings was to cut the number of books and purchase more computers. 20% of books were sold off or given away, the space given over to additional computer tables, and the library’s entire available budget given over to purchasing new computers.
Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the librarian’s reasoning?

main_body.text: In a survey done by a school librarian during one year, borrowing of books in the library declined by 20%. Amongst books borrowed, rates of late return or loss of books also increased by 10%. On the other hand, student use of computers in the library increased by 25%. This finding was reinforced by frequent complaints from students that there were no computers available when they needed to use them. The librarian concluded that the best response to these findings was to cut the number of books and purchase more computers. 20% of books were sold off or given away, the space given over to additional computer tables, and the library’s entire available budget given over to purchasing new computers.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the librarian’s reasoning?

options.label: A
options.text: The library should cater for the students’ preferences rather than trying to change them.

options.label: B
options.text: A decline in the borrowing of books indicates a decline in reading.

options.label: C
options.text: Students were unjustified in complaining about the lack of computers.

options.label: D
options.text: Students’ educational achievement is improved by using computers.

options.label: E
options.text: Library use will necessarily increase if more computers are provided.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The librarian observes that book borrowing has declined while computer use has increased, accompanied by complaints about insufficient computer availability. She responds by removing books and spending the library's entire available budget on additional computers.

This decision assumes that the library should adapt its resources to students' demonstrated preferences rather than attempt to influence those preferences or preserve existing resources for other purposes. Without that principle, increased computer demand would not automatically justify reallocating resources away from books. Therefore, A is the underlying assumption.

items.label: B
items.text: Declining library borrowing does not necessarily mean students are reading less, since they might obtain books elsewhere. The decision to provide more computers does not require assuming an overall decline in reading.

items.label: C
items.text: The librarian treats complaints about unavailable computers as evidence of demand. Assuming those complaints were unjustified would weaken rather than support her response.

items.label: D
items.text: The argument does not establish or require that computers improve educational achievement. It bases resource allocation on usage and expressed demand.

items.label: E
items.text: The librarian can respond to existing demand without assuming that providing more computers will necessarily increase total library usage.

Recently, packets of Amblers crisps have had ‘money-off’ coupons inside them. Some coupons are worth 9p, some are worth 14p and some are worth 20p.
George has been collecting these coupons. He has more 14p coupons than 9p coupons, and more 9p coupons than 20p coupons. The total value of all of his coupons is exactly £1.50.
How many coupons has George collected?

main_body.text:
Recently, packets of Amblers crisps have had ‘money-off’ coupons inside them. Some coupons are worth 9p, some are worth 14p and some are worth 20p.
George has been collecting these coupons. He has more 14p coupons than 9p coupons, and more 9p coupons than 20p coupons. The total value of all of his coupons is exactly £1.50.

question_view.main_question: How many coupons has George collected?

notes: White background/decorative object retained in question preview.
White background/decorative object retained in question preview.

blocks.text:
Let a, b and c be the numbers of 9p, 14p and 20p coupons. Their total value is 150p, so 9a + 14b + 20c = 150, with b > a > c.

Since the total is even, a must be even. Also, b ≥ a + 1, so 9a + 14(a + 1) ≤ 150, restricting a to 2 or 4. If a = 4, then 7b + 10c = 57, requiring b to end in 1, which is incompatible with b > 4 and the total value. Thus a = 2. The equation becomes 7b + 10c = 66, giving b = 8 and c = 1.

The counts satisfy 8 > 2 > 1, and the value is 8(14) + 2(9) + 1(20) = 150p. Total coupons = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11. Therefore, C is correct.

items.label: A
items.text: With 9 coupons, the value equation permits counts of 0 nine-penny, 5 fourteen-penny and 4 twenty-penny coupons, but these violate the required ordering.

items.label: B
items.text: With 10 coupons, the compatible value counts are 4 nine-penny, 1 fourteen-penny and 5 twenty-penny coupons. The fourteen-penny count is not the largest.

items.label: D
items.text: With 12 coupons, the value equation gives 6 nine-penny, 4 fourteen-penny and 2 twenty-penny coupons. This violates b > a.

items.label: E
items.text: With 13 coupons, the value equation gives 10 nine-penny, 0 fourteen-penny and 3 twenty-penny coupons, contradicting the required ordering.

main_body.text: Welfare benefits create a culture of dependency and an unproductive workforce. There are people who stay on welfare benefits for years and never look for employment. Two years ago the government introduced tougher restrictions on the eligibility to receive benefits and the number of recipients has now fallen by 20%. The government should therefore toughen these restrictions even more to further reduce the number of welfare claimants.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following identifies the flaw in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: It rests on the false assumption that people are happy to stay on benefits and not look for work.

options.label: B

options.text: It ignores the possibility of other causes for the fall in the number of welfare recipients.

blocks.text:
The argument notes that welfare restrictions became tougher two years ago and that the number of benefit recipients subsequently fell by 20%. It then recommends further restrictions, treating the reduction as evidence that the policy worked and that additional restrictions will produce further reductions.

However, the sequence of events does not establish that the restrictions caused the entire decline. Other factors could have contributed to the reduction in recipient numbers. Without establishing the actual cause, the argument cannot reliably predict that stricter rules will produce the desired result. Therefore, C identifies the flaw.

items.label: B

items.label: D
items.text: The argument associates long-term welfare dependency with an unproductive workforce, but its policy inference specifically depends on the unexplained relationship between restrictions and reduced recipient numbers.

items.label: E
items.text: The passage does not establish that every recipient is personally responsible for requiring benefits. Nevertheless, the specific failure in the proposed policy argument is its unsupported causal inference.

question_view.question_text:
There seems to be universal agreement on Shakespeare’s greatness, yet many of his plays lack any significant development of plot or character. An exceptional skill with language is evident in all his works and his running theme concerning the relationship between appearances and reality has appealed to audiences across times and cultures. But is this enough to confer greatness? More likely this status derives from a small number of his plays, the four great tragedies, which succeed in dramatising reflection on the depths of the human condition. It is this which touches the hearts and minds of his audience.
Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

main_body.text: There seems to be universal agreement on Shakespeare’s greatness, yet many of his plays lack any significant development of plot or character. An exceptional skill with language is evident in all his works and his running theme concerning the relationship between appearances and reality has appealed to audiences across times and cultures. But is this enough to confer greatness? More likely this status derives from a small number of his plays, the four great tragedies, which succeed in dramatising reflection on the depths of the human condition. It is this which touches the hearts and minds of his audience.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Shakespeare’s focus on the relationship between appearances and reality has appealed to audiences across times and cultures.

options.label: B
options.text: There seems to be universal agreement on Shakespeare’s greatness.

options.label: C
options.text: Shakespeare succeeds in touching the hearts and minds of audiences.

options.label: D
options.text: Shakespeare’s greatness derives from a small number of his plays, the great tragedies.

options.label: E
options.text: Limited plot and character development in many of his plays do not affect Shakespeare’s reputation as a great playwright.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The passage acknowledges Shakespeare's reputation and linguistic skill but questions whether these qualities alone explain his greatness, especially since many plays lack substantial plot or character development.

It proposes that his exceptional status instead derives chiefly from a small group of works: the four great tragedies. These plays are distinguished by their exploration of fundamental aspects of human existence, which enables them to affect audiences deeply. Therefore, D expresses the main conclusion: Shakespeare's greatness derives from a small number of his plays, particularly the great tragedies.

items.text: The enduring appeal of Shakespeare's treatment of appearances and reality is acknowledged as a characteristic of his writing, but the author argues that another feature better explains his greatness.

items.label: B
items.text: The apparent agreement about Shakespeare's greatness establishes the issue that the passage seeks to explain. It is the starting point rather than the conclusion.

items.label: C
items.text: The emotional and intellectual impact of Shakespeare's tragedies explains why these particular plays account for his greatness. It is supporting reasoning rather than the complete conclusion.

items.label: E
items.text: The passage notes limited development of plot and character in many plays but does not conclude that these limitations have no effect on Shakespeare's reputation.

How long after I arrived at the booth did I insert my money?

Money may only be inserted when the green light is on. This light goes out immediately after money is inserted, and comes back on again exactly 3 minutes later.

The green light returns exactly 3 minutes after money is inserted, so consecutive customers can pay at 3-minute intervals. The first person inserts money immediately upon the booth opening, at 0 minutes.

As sixth in the queue, the narrator must wait for five earlier customers to insert their money. Their payment times are 0, 3, 6, 9 and 12 minutes. question_view.question_text:
Modern aeroplanes are for the most part ‘flown’ by autoflight computers. These computers can take over when the plane is just 30 metres off the ground, maintain whatever speed and height is tapped into the flight management system, and land the aircraft automatically. But when autoflight computers experience situations they haven’t been programmed to handle – sudden structural damage to the aircraft, or extreme weather – they can throw back responsibility to the pilot, who may become confused over the level of control they have. The confusion is made worse by flight deck computers overloading pilots with a blizzard of alerts. This is when crashes are most likely to happen.
Which one of the following is a conclusion that can be drawn from the above passage?

main_body.text: Modern aeroplanes are for the most part ‘flown’ by autoflight computers. These computers can take over when the plane is just 30 metres off the ground, maintain whatever speed and height is tapped into the flight management system, and land the aircraft automatically. But when autoflight computers experience situations they haven’t been programmed to handle – sudden structural damage to the aircraft, or extreme weather – they can throw back responsibility to the pilot, who may become confused over the level of control they have. The confusion is made worse by flight deck computers overloading pilots with a blizzard of alerts. This is when crashes are most likely to happen.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is a conclusion that can be drawn from the above passage?

options.label: A
options.text: Developing autoflight computers further to allow pilotless planes is likely to be safer than the current arrangement.

options.label: B
options.text: Automated systems can be refined to the extent that air crashes will not happen.

options.label: C
options.text: The combination of computer and human control over an aircraft is unsafe in most situations.

options.label: D
options.text: Autoflight computers can be controlled as easily from the ground as from inside the plane.

options.label: E
options.text: Human error in entering data into autoflight computers will always pose a risk.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The passage identifies a particular danger in the current arrangement: when autoflight computers encounter unexpected situations, they may transfer control to pilots who are confused about their responsibilities and overwhelmed by alerts. Crashes are described as most likely during this breakdown in coordination.

A draws the inference that further development towards fully pilotless aircraft could reduce this danger by removing the problematic transfer between automated and human control. It is a prediction rather than a guarantee of safety, but it most directly follows from the identified weakness of the current combined system.

items.label: B
items.text: The passage identifies situations that existing systems cannot handle, but it provides no basis for claiming that further automation could eliminate every possible cause of an aircraft crash.

items.label: C
items.text: The passage locates the greatest danger in exceptional situations involving failed coordination. It does not claim that combining human and computer control is unsafe in most ordinary situations.

items.label: D
items.text: The passage discusses onboard flight computers and pilots but provides no information about controlling aircraft remotely from the ground.

items.label: E
items.text: The identified danger concerns unexpected situations, unclear control responsibilities and excessive alerts. The passage does not attribute crashes to incorrectly entered data or establish that such errors will always occur.

Children spend far too long in schools analysing poems when they should simply be learning to enjoy them. Thankfully, a new approach requires that, instead of focusing on analysing technical aspects of writing such as the writer’s use of imagery or alliteration, children will be required simply to learn poems so that they can recite them by heart. This makes good sense.
What is the use of learning how to analyse literature if you have no appreciation of its actual value? If they then become interested in it enough to study it at A level or at university, that can be when they learn to analyse in detail the author’s craft.
Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

main_body.text:
Children spend far too long in schools analysing poems when they should simply be learning to enjoy them. Thankfully, a new approach requires that, instead of focusing on analysing technical aspects of writing such as the writer’s use of imagery or alliteration, children will be required simply to learn poems so that they can recite them by heart. This makes good sense.
What is the use of learning how to analyse literature if you have no appreciation of its actual value? If they then become interested in it enough to study it at A level or at university, that can be when they learn to analyse in detail the author’s craft.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Analysing the writer’s craft could enhance the appreciation of the poem.

options.label: B
options.text: Children are not currently required to learn poems off by heart.

options.label: C
options.text: English will continue to be a subject available for study at A level or university.

options.label: D
options.text: For something to be classed as poetry it must include either alliteration or imagery.

options.label: E
options.text: Learning a poem off by heart will enable you to appreciate it more.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument recommends replacing detailed literary analysis with memorisation and recitation because it believes children should develop an appreciation of poetry before studying its technical features.

For memorisation to be a suitable replacement, learning poems by heart must help children appreciate them. Otherwise, removing detailed analysis in favour of recitation would not necessarily achieve the objective of making poetry more enjoyable or valuable to students. Therefore, E is the underlying assumption linking the proposed teaching method to its intended benefit.

items.label: A
items.text: The possibility that literary analysis improves appreciation could favour retaining analysis. The argument does not require this benefit to exist before recommending memorisation.

items.label: B
items.text: The passage contrasts an existing emphasis on analysis with a new requirement to memorise poems, but the argument does not depend on proving that no children currently memorise poetry.

items.label: C
items.text: The availability of advanced literary study is mentioned as a possible later stage. The recommendation to develop appreciation first does not depend on the continued existence of every particular qualification.

items.label: D
items.text: Imagery and alliteration are examples of techniques studied in literary analysis. The argument does not require either technique to be present in every poem.

The financial circumstances of many young people make it difficult for them to forego paid employment for an extended period in order to undertake unpaid internships or work experience placements. In many industries, it is unlikely that a young person will gain entry-
level paid employment unless he or she has held one of these temporary unpaid positions.
Therefore, the current system of unpaid internships creates an unfair advantage for individuals from more affluent backgrounds.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Unpaid internships and work experience placements often provide young people with an important opportunity for gaining references.

options.label: B
options.text: The highest proportion of unpaid internships and work experience placements are based in a few central locations, such as London.

options.label: C
options.text: Unpaid internships and work experience placements come in various lengths of duration from one to two days up to a number of months.

options.label: D
options.text: Some young people find themselves moving from one unpaid position to another without being able to land a paid job.

options.label: E
options.text: Some schools and other organisations have programmes in place to help match young people with internships or work experience placements.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument claims that unpaid internships unfairly favour wealthier young people because entry-level jobs often require experience that less affluent applicants cannot afford to obtain through extended periods of unpaid work.

C weakens this reasoning by establishing that internships vary considerably in duration, with some lasting only one or two days. Short placements may not require applicants to sacrifice paid employment for an extended period, reducing the force of the financial barrier described. This does not eliminate all inequality, but it challenges the assumption that obtaining relevant unpaid experience necessarily requires a prolonged financial sacrifice.

items.label: D
items.text: Some interns repeatedly failing to obtain paid work raises doubts about the effectiveness of internships, but it does not demonstrate that poorer applicants have equal access to them.

items.label: E

question_view.question_text:
In the main draw of a lottery, six of the balls (which are numbered from 1 to 49) are selected at random, then the numbers chosen are rearranged and displayed in ascending numerical order.
For instance: 3 17 20 29 34 45
In one draw recently, I noticed that the six numbers were made up of a total of ten digits, all different. The lowest number on this occasion was 1 and the highest number was 49, so the range of the six numbers was 48, the greatest possible range for the lottery main draw.
What is the smallest possible range when the six numbers in the main draw of the lottery have a total of ten digits, all different?

main_body.text:
In the main draw of a lottery, six of the balls (which are numbered from 1 to 49) are selected at random, then the numbers chosen are rearranged and displayed in ascending numerical order.
For instance: 3 17 20 29 34 45
In one draw recently, I noticed that the six numbers were made up of a total of ten digits, all different. The lowest number on this occasion was 1 and the highest number was 49, so the range of the six numbers was 48, the greatest possible range for the lottery main draw.

question_view.main_question: What is the smallest possible range when the six numbers in the main draw of the lottery have a total of ten digits, all different?

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
Six numbers containing ten distinct digits must consist of two single-digit and four two-digit numbers. Because all ten digits are different, the four two-digit numbers must use distinct tens digits. Within the lottery's range of 1–49, those tens digits must be 1, 2, 3 and 4. Therefore, the largest number is at least 40.

The two distinct single-digit numbers must include one no greater than 8, so the smallest number is at most 8. Hence the range cannot be less than 40 − 8 = 32.

This minimum is achievable with 8, 9, 15, 26, 37 and 40. Their ten digits are all different, and the range is 40 − 8 = 32. Therefore, E is correct.

items.label: A
items.text: A range of 21 is smaller than the proven minimum of 32, which follows from the necessary presence of a number at least 40 and another at most 8.

items.label: B
items.text: A range of 23 cannot accommodate the required four distinct two-digit tens digits and two distinct single-digit numbers.

items.label: C
items.text: A range of 27 is below the minimum separation of 32 between the largest and smallest numbers.

items.label: D
items.text: 31 is one less than the theoretical minimum. The required largest number is at least 40 and the smallest is at most 8, giving a difference of at least 32.

question_view.question_text:
Charities address the negative effects of market economies, which apportion goods to people based on their ability to pay as opposed to their needs. The work of charities conceals the true impact of the market system and, worse, leaves the market in place to produce further negative outcomes. Charities therefore effectively perpetuate the problems the market system creates. Since it is immoral to support a practice that perpetuates the very problems it is supposed to resolve, giving to charity cannot be morally justified. After all, if the effects of a system are morally wrong, then it is immoral to sustain that system.
Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

main_body.text: Charities address the negative effects of market economies, which apportion goods to people based on their ability to pay as opposed to their needs. The work of charities conceals the true impact of the market system and, worse, leaves the market in place to produce further negative outcomes. Charities therefore effectively perpetuate the problems the market system creates. Since it is immoral to support a practice that perpetuates the very problems it is supposed to resolve, giving to charity cannot be morally justified. After all, if the effects of a system are morally wrong, then it is immoral to sustain that system.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Charity does not address the cause of the problem.

options.label: B
options.text: Charitable giving is necessary because of the market system.

options.label: C
options.text: Charities perpetuate the negative effects of market economies.

options.label: D
options.text: Giving to charity is immoral.

options.label: E
options.text: Charities conceal the negative effects of the operation of the market.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument claims that charities relieve the negative consequences of market economies without correcting the underlying system responsible for those consequences. By concealing the system's harmful effects and allowing it to continue, charities are said to perpetuate the very problems they seek to solve.

The author then applies a moral principle: supporting a system that perpetuates harmful outcomes is immoral. Since charitable giving allegedly sustains such a system, the author concludes that giving to charity cannot be morally justified. Therefore, D expresses the main conclusion.

items.label: A
items.text: The claim that charity does not address the underlying cause is part of the argument explaining why charitable activity allegedly perpetuates problems. It is not the final moral conclusion.

items.label: B
items.text: The passage connects the existence of charities to problems created by market economies, but it does not conclude that charitable giving is necessary or desirable.

items.label: C
items.text: The alleged perpetuation of market-related harms is an intermediate conclusion used to justify the broader judgement about the morality of charitable giving.

items.label: E
items.text: The claim that charities conceal the negative consequences of the market is supporting evidence for the argument that they sustain the system.

You can only grasp the true meaning of Pushkin’s poetry if you can read it in its original Russian form. Your doctoral thesis on Pushkin’s work shows acute insight so I can tell you have a mastery of the Russian language.
Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

main_body.text: You can only grasp the true meaning of Pushkin’s poetry if you can read it in its original Russian form. Your doctoral thesis on Pushkin’s work shows acute insight so I can tell you have a mastery of the Russian language.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Only when there is a clear sky will you be able to practice some astronomy. Tonight is forecast to be cloudless so you will be able to do some stargazing.

options.label: B
options.text: You have to place your dustbin on the street outside before 8a.m. today for the refuse collectors to deal with it. Since you put yours in the correct place at 7a.m. your dustbin will be emptied.

options.label: C
options.text: You have to score at the 98th percentile or higher in a standardised IQ test to become a member of Mensa. As you are not a member of Mensa it is clear that your IQ falls outside the top 2%.

options.label: D
options.text: Only towns that have a bypass to divert their traffic are able to create a pedestrian-only high street for local shoppers. I see your town has the benefit of traffic-free shopping, so the bypass must now be open.

options.label: E
options.text: You need to have 45 hours in the air before you can take a pilot’s licence test. You have only flown 18 hours so you will not be able to take the test.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The original argument states that understanding the true meaning of Pushkin's poetry requires being able to read the original Russian. It then treats the doctoral thesis's acute insight as evidence that the writer possesses this understanding and concludes that the writer must know Russian.

D follows the same structure: a pedestrian-only high street requires a bypass, and the town has pedestrian-only shopping, so the argument concludes that the bypass must exist. Both infer a necessary condition from the presence of an outcome that supposedly requires it.

items.label: A
items.text: A clear sky is presented as necessary for astronomy, but the argument treats having a clear sky as sufficient to guarantee stargazing. This reverses the direction of the original reasoning.

items.label: B
items.text: Putting the dustbin out before 8 a.m. is stated as necessary for collection, but the argument incorrectly treats satisfying that requirement as sufficient to guarantee collection.

items.label: C
items.text: The Mensa argument infers the absence of a required qualification from non-membership. Failure to obtain membership does not establish that the IQ requirement was not met.

items.label: E
items.text: Having 45 flying hours is required before taking the test, and having only 18 hours establishes that this requirement is unmet. It reasons from the absence of a necessary condition, rather than inferring its presence from an observed outcome.

question_view.question_text:
It has emerged that prisoners have helped to maintain one of Britain’s busiest railway lines.
Inmates from an open prison have worked night-shifts on the main line from London to Glasgow. This is the same line where a train left the tracks earlier this year, killing one person and injuring several others. It is all very well to have offenders being rehabilitated through work, but what appears to be happening here is that rail contractors are cynically using prisoners as cheap labour. This is unacceptable, not just for safety reasons – important as they are – but because ultimately it is an infringement of workers’ rights. If these prisoners are being paid less, or treated differently from regular workers, the practice must stop once and for all.
Which one of the following expresses the general principle that underlies the above argument?

main_body.text:
It has emerged that prisoners have helped to maintain one of Britain’s busiest railway lines.
Inmates from an open prison have worked night-shifts on the main line from London to Glasgow. This is the same line where a train left the tracks earlier this year, killing one person and injuring several others. It is all very well to have offenders being rehabilitated through work, but what appears to be happening here is that rail contractors are cynically using prisoners as cheap labour. This is unacceptable, not just for safety reasons – important as they are – but because ultimately it is an infringement of workers’ rights. If these prisoners are being paid less, or treated differently from regular workers, the practice must stop once and for all.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following expresses the general principle that underlies the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Labour is labour and should have the same value whoever is performing it.

options.label: B
options.text: Public safety issues must always be given priority over economic advantages.

options.label: C
options.text: Rehabilitation should be for the prisoner’s benefit, not the employer’s.

options.label: D
options.text: Prisoners who are given work should not take jobs away from other workers.

options.label: E
options.text: Maintenance of public services should be in the hands of skilled professionals only.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument accepts that prisoners may benefit from rehabilitation through work but condemns using them as cheap labour if this means they receive lower pay or worse treatment than ordinary workers. The objection is therefore not to prisoners working, but to their labour being valued differently merely because of their prisoner status.

A expresses the general principle underlying this criticism: work should receive equivalent value and treatment regardless of who performs it. This explains why unequal treatment of prisoners and regular workers would make the arrangement unacceptable.

items.label: B
items.text: Public safety is mentioned as a concern, but the argument explicitly identifies workers' rights as an additional and ultimately decisive objection to the arrangement.

items.label: C
items.text: Rehabilitation is recognised as a legitimate purpose of prison work, but the argument does not require employers to receive no benefit. Its objection concerns unfair treatment and compensation.

items.label: D
items.text: The passage does not establish that prisoners are replacing regular employees. Its concern is that prisoners may be treated less favourably for performing work.

items.label: E
items.text: The passage raises safety concerns but does not establish that prisoners necessarily lack relevant skills or that only particular professional groups should maintain public services.

A car journey begins with a 15km drive at an average speed of 60km/hour, then 5hours on the motorway, including two 15-minute rest stops, travelling at an average driving speed of
80km/hour, and finally a 20km drive at an average speed of 40km/hour from the motorway to the destination.
If the destination is reached at 12:00midday, at what time did the journey begin?

main_body.text:
A car journey begins with a 15km drive at an average speed of 60km/hour, then 5hours on the motorway, including two 15-minute rest stops, travelling at an average driving speed of
80km/hour, and finally a 20km drive at an average speed of 40km/hour from the motorway to the destination.

question_view.main_question: If the destination is reached at 12:00midday, at what time did the journey begin?

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The journey consists of three sections. The first 15km at 60km/h takes 15 ÷ 60 = 0.25 hours, or 15 minutes. The motorway section takes 5 hours in total, including the two 15-minute rest stops. The final 20km at 40km/h takes 20 ÷ 40 = 0.5 hours, or 30 minutes.

Total journey time = 15 minutes + 5 hours + 30 minutes = 5 hours 45 minutes. Subtracting this duration from the arrival time of 12:00 midday gives a departure time of 06:15. Therefore, D is correct.

items.label: A
items.text: 05:18 would give a journey lasting 6 hours 42 minutes, exceeding the stated total by 57 minutes.

items.label: B
items.text: 05:25 would give 6 hours 35 minutes of travel, which is 50 minutes longer than the calculated duration.

items.label: C
items.text: 05:45 would imply a 6-hour-15-minute journey, adding 30 minutes to the stated duration. The two rest stops are already included in the motorway's 5 hours.

items.label: E
items.text: 06:45 would provide only 5 hours 15 minutes before arrival, which is 30 minutes shorter than the required journey.

Like other booming cities, including New York, London has thrived amid globalisation. It is growing by 100000 new residents a year. However, if London has given striving people plenty of reasons to come, it has done a poor job of housing them. The median price of a London home has tripled over the past two decades. Since 2001 the disposable income of people renting property has fallen by 30 per cent as a result. Businesses are worried too. Commercial property in central London is twice as expensive as in New York. Productivity has begun to slow as promising firms are forced out. Overpriced property is costing London the economic and human diversity on which its prosperity depends.
Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

main_body.text: Like other booming cities, including New York, London has thrived amid globalisation. It is growing by 100000 new residents a year. However, if London has given striving people plenty of reasons to come, it has done a poor job of housing them. The median price of a London home has tripled over the past two decades. Since 2001 the disposable income of people renting property has fallen by 30 per cent as a result. Businesses are worried too. Commercial property in central London is twice as expensive as in New York. Productivity has begun to slow as promising firms are forced out. Overpriced property is costing London the economic and human diversity on which its prosperity depends.

question_view.question_text:
A high degree of self-discipline is one quality exhibited by all athletes who have reached the uppermost levels of competition, whatever the sport. This amount of self-discipline is in evidence long after the initial excitement of a sport has worn off, and an athlete has had to keep going through years of painful and repetitive training sessions. The example of top athletes suggests one approach to improving student behaviour and educational achievement.
If more young people could begin training programmes akin to those of elite athletes, they too would develop exceptional levels of personal discipline to apply within their studies.
Which one of the following best expresses the flaw in the above argument?

main_body.text:
A high degree of self-discipline is one quality exhibited by all athletes who have reached the uppermost levels of competition, whatever the sport. This amount of self-discipline is in evidence long after the initial excitement of a sport has worn off, and an athlete has had to keep going through years of painful and repetitive training sessions. The example of top athletes suggests one approach to improving student behaviour and educational achievement.
If more young people could begin training programmes akin to those of elite athletes, they too would develop exceptional levels of personal discipline to apply within their studies.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the flaw in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: High levels of self-discipline may not be all that it takes to become an elite athlete.

options.label: B
options.text: Young people may be able to develop self-discipline through other kinds of activities.

options.label: C
options.text: The kind of coaching support available to elite athletes may not be accessible to the general population.

options.label: D
options.text: Good behaviour and educational achievement during one’s school years may not be essential for going on to lead a successful life.

options.label: E
options.text: Strong self-discipline may not be an effect of the training but rather a capacity already possessed by athletes as they start their training.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument observes that elite athletes demonstrate exceptional self-discipline after years of demanding training. It then assumes that their training developed this discipline and concludes that similar programmes would produce comparable discipline in students.

However, the observed relationship does not establish causation. Athletes may already possess unusually strong self-discipline before beginning training, enabling them to persist through difficult programmes and reach elite levels. If so, training might not produce the same discipline in students who lack this initial characteristic. Therefore, E identifies the flaw: confusing a pre-existing characteristic with an effect of training.

items.label: A
items.text: Elite performance may require abilities beyond self-discipline, but the argument concerns whether training develops discipline, not whether discipline alone guarantees sporting success.

items.label: B
items.text: Other activities might also develop self-discipline, but this does not undermine the possibility that athletic training could develop it.

items.label: C
items.text: Limited access to elite coaching could make similar programmes difficult to implement. However, this is a practical obstacle rather than the underlying causal error about how athletes acquire discipline.

items.label: D
items.text: Educational achievement may not be necessary for success in later life, but this does not address whether athletic training would improve students' discipline or academic performance.

Adults thinking back on their experience of school almost always remember with most gratitude the teachers who taught them more than just a subject, and prepared them for life, not just for an exam. But the current generation of students may not have the same experiences to look back on in future years because the role of teachers has changed. The focus for both students and teachers is now mainly on exam results, and that is how their success or failure is measured. For teachers to share their lives with their students, offering them a model of adulthood to which to aspire, is therefore no longer considered desirable. So children today receive a less valuable education than their parents and grandparents did.
Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

main_body.text: Adults thinking back on their experience of school almost always remember with most gratitude the teachers who taught them more than just a subject, and prepared them for life, not just for an exam. But the current generation of students may not have the same experiences to look back on in future years because the role of teachers has changed. The focus for both students and teachers is now mainly on exam results, and that is how their success or failure is measured. For teachers to share their lives with their students, offering them a model of adulthood to which to aspire, is therefore no longer considered desirable. So children today receive a less valuable education than their parents and grandparents did.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Many young people have higher ambitions than becoming like their teachers.

options.label: D
options.text: Exam results are the vital keys which open the door to education and a livelihood.

options.text: Offering students a model of adulthood is a more satisfying role than helping them to pass exams.

blocks.text:
The argument claims that education today is less valuable because teachers increasingly focus on examination results rather than preparing students for life and providing examples of adulthood.

For this change to constitute a reduction in educational value, preparation for life must be considered more valuable than merely achieving examination success. If examination results were equally or more important, the shift towards exam-focused teaching would not necessarily make education worse. Therefore, A is the underlying assumption connecting the change in teaching priorities to the conclusion about reduced educational value.

items.label: B
items.text: Adults may selectively remember positive school experiences, but the argument does not require this tendency. Such bias could instead weaken the comparison with earlier generations.

items.label: C
items.text: Students may have ambitions different from those of their teachers, but the argument concerns the value of learning from adult role models, not necessarily copying their careers or ambitions.

items.label: D
items.text: Examination results may be important for future opportunities, but this does not establish that exam-focused education is more valuable than broader preparation for life.

items.label: E
items.text: The argument concerns the educational benefits received by students, not whether teachers find mentoring more personally satisfying than helping students pass examinations.

Texting is the preferred method of communication among young people, with 72% of teenagers saying they text regularly and one in three sending more than a hundred texts per day.
Unfortunately, however, very few youngsters seem able to communicate using grammatically correct sentences. They seem to think it ‘gr8’ that correct spelling is no longer considered necessary. Many local employers have complained that school-leavers have no idea how to communicate appropriately, whether face-to-face or in business letters. Many written job applications are phrased so poorly that they go straight in the bin. Mobile phones were banned in my daughter’s school last year, a move which has proved fully justified. Since then test scores in English have improved. All schools need to introduce a similar ban.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the flaw in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: It makes a false statistical comparison between the 72% of teenagers who merely text regularly and those who send more than a hundred texts in a day.

options.label: B
options.text: It assumes that, because test scores improved after the ban on mobile phones, the improvement was due to the ban.

options.label: C
options.text: The argument rests on the assumption that communicating by text is inappropriate.

options.label: D
options.text: Its conclusion, that communicating by text is inappropriate, merely restates one of the reasons given in support of the argument.

options.label: E
options.text: It assumes that correct spelling is a necessary requirement for gaining employment.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument states that mobile phones were banned in the author's daughter's school and that English test scores subsequently improved. It treats this sequence as evidence that the ban caused the improvement and uses it to recommend equivalent bans in every school.

However, an improvement occurring after a policy change does not establish that the policy caused it. Other changes in teaching, assessment or student performance could explain the higher scores. Without identifying the cause, the argument cannot reliably attribute the improvement to the phone ban. Therefore, B identifies the flaw.

items.label: A
items.text: The two texting statistics describe different frequencies of texting, but the argument does not make the statistical comparison alleged. Its decisive inference concerns the cause of improved examination scores.

items.label: C
items.text: The passage criticises poor spelling and inappropriate communication, not necessarily every use of text messaging. The proposed ban depends on the claimed educational benefits rather than treating all texting as inherently inappropriate.

items.label: D
items.text: The main conclusion recommends banning mobile phones in schools, not that texting itself is inappropriate. The argument therefore does not merely restate a premise as its conclusion.

items.label: E
items.text: Poor spelling may harm job applications, but the passage does not establish that perfect spelling is required for every job. This stronger assumption is unnecessary to the argument about school phone bans.

While it is a woman, Ada Lovelace, who is often credited with originating the concept of software, today’s computer tech-related jobs are held mostly by men. The tech sector must continue to work against factors that inhibit gender equality within it. One such factor appears to be prejudice about women’s abilities to write computer programming code. A recent study of a program-sharing and development website analysed the rates by which suggested code changes were accepted by website users according to the gender of the user contributing the changes. In cases where the contributor’s gender was not made clear on the website, 72 per cent of the suggestions made by women were accepted. In cases where the contributor’s gender was revealed to be female, the acceptance rate fell to 63 per cent.
Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

main_body.text: While it is a woman, Ada Lovelace, who is often credited with originating the concept of software, today’s computer tech-related jobs are held mostly by men. The tech sector must continue to work against factors that inhibit gender equality within it. One such factor appears to be prejudice about women’s abilities to write computer programming code. A recent study of a program-sharing and development website analysed the rates by which suggested code changes were accepted by website users according to the gender of the user contributing the changes. In cases where the contributor’s gender was not made clear on the website, 72 per cent of the suggestions made by women were accepted. In cases where the contributor’s gender was revealed to be female, the acceptance rate fell to 63 per cent.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Over the time period the website was studied, more female users than male users rejected suggested code changes overall.

options.label: B
options.text: Leading firms in the tech sector have undertaken a variety of high-profile initiatives to encourage more women to pursue computer programming careers.

options.label: C
options.text: No meaningful differences existed between the code changes suggested by female users who revealed their gender on the website and those who did not.

options.label: D
options.text: Even by modern standards, Ada Lovelace received an extensive education in mathematics and the sciences.

options.label: E
options.text: Male contributors to the website experienced a similar drop in their code change acceptance rates when their gender was revealed.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument suggests prejudice against female programmers because code changes submitted by women were accepted 72% of the time when their gender was hidden, compared with 63% when it was revealed.

However, E states that male contributors experienced a similar decline when their gender became visible. This introduces an alternative explanation: revealing a contributor's gender, or the associated visibility of their identity, may affect acceptance rates generally rather than reflecting prejudice specifically against women. Therefore, E most weakens the inference that the observed decline demonstrates gender-specific discrimination against female programmers.

items.text: Female users rejecting more code changes concerns their behaviour as reviewers, not whether other users discriminate against female contributors whose gender is visible.

items.label: B
items.text: Initiatives encouraging women to enter programming show efforts to improve representation, but they do not establish whether bias affected the acceptance rates in the study.

items.label: C
items.text: If the two groups of female contributors submitted code of similar quality, differences in the code itself would become a less plausible explanation for the acceptance-rate gap. This would strengthen the discrimination hypothesis.

items.label: D
items.text: Ada Lovelace's scientific education provides historical background but does not explain the difference between acceptance rates for identified and unidentified female contributors.

question_view.question_text:
When riding my bike in the dark, I use two rear bike lamps. Both of the lamps are in ‘flashing mode’, which means that they repeatedly emit light for a set period of time at set intervals. The reasons for using two lights are that it reduces the amount of time when neither of the lamps emit light, and that if one of the lamps stops working, other road users can still see me on the road. One of the lamps shines for one second and goes dark for one second repeatedly; the other lamp shines for two seconds and goes dark for two seconds repeatedly. I always turn both lamps on simultaneously at the start of my ride.
For how many seconds in each minute do neither of the lamps shine when they are in use?
question_view.main_question:
When riding my bike in the dark, I use two rear bike lamps. Both of the lamps are in ‘flashing mode’, which means that they repeatedly emit light for a set period of time at set intervals. The reasons for using two lights are that it reduces the amount of time when neither of the lamps emit light, and that if one of the lamps stops working, other road users can still see me on the road. One of the lamps shines for one second and goes dark for one second repeatedly; the other lamp shines for two seconds and goes dark for two seconds repeatedly. I always turn both lamps on simultaneously at the start of my ride.
For how many seconds in each minute do neither of the lamps shine when they are in use?

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The first lamp alternates between 1 second on and 1 second off, repeating every 2 seconds. The second alternates between 2 seconds on and 2 seconds off, repeating every 4 seconds. Both are switched on simultaneously.

Over each 4-second cycle, the first lamp is off during seconds 1–2 and 3–4, while the second is off during seconds 2–4. Therefore, both lamps are off together only during seconds 3–4, for exactly 1 second per 4-second cycle.

There are 60 ÷ 4 = 15 complete cycles in one minute, giving 15 × 1 = 15 seconds of simultaneous darkness. Therefore, C is correct.

items.label: A
items.text: 10 seconds would represent only one-sixth of a minute, whereas the repeating patterns produce simultaneous darkness for one-quarter of every 4-second cycle.

items.label: B
items.text: 12 seconds is 3 seconds below the calculated total and does not match the 15 identical cycles occurring each minute.

items.label: D
items.text: 20 seconds exceeds the established duration by 5 seconds. Both lamps are dark together for only 1 second in each 4-second cycle.

items.label: E
items.text: 30 seconds is the total time each individual lamp spends switched off during a minute. It does not account for the other lamp remaining illuminated during some of those intervals.

Recently a pioneering natural flood management scheme slowed river peak flow by 15 to
20 per cent, saving a small town’s museum and several homes. As part of this scheme, special dams, designed to leak water gradually, were installed in nearby hills to slow the flow of water off the slopes. An upstream flood storage reservoir was installed, along with the planting of thousands of trees and the restoration of heather moorland, which acted as a sponge. Around half of the reduction in flood water in the town was due to the upstream land management measures, and half due to the effect of the flood storage area. Natural flood management measures improve water quality, prevent erosion and, in some cases, store carbon.
Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?

main_body.text:
Recently a pioneering natural flood management scheme slowed river peak flow by 15 to
20 per cent, saving a small town’s museum and several homes. As part of this scheme, special dams, designed to leak water gradually, were installed in nearby hills to slow the flow of water off the slopes. An upstream flood storage reservoir was installed, along with the planting of thousands of trees and the restoration of heather moorland, which acted as a sponge. Around half of the reduction in flood water in the town was due to the upstream land management measures, and half due to the effect of the flood storage area. Natural flood management measures improve water quality, prevent erosion and, in some cases, store carbon.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?

options.label: A
options.text: The reduction in peak flow of a river would be insufficient to prevent flooding if there was very heavy rainfall.

options.label: B
options.text: The benefits of natural flood management schemes go beyond reducing flood risk.

options.label: C
options.text: All natural flood management methods are equally effective in reducing river flow.

options.label: D
options.text: Natural flood management should be introduced in all areas at risk of flooding.

options.label: E
options.text: Natural flood management methods are most effective in hilly upland areas.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The passage describes a natural flood management scheme that successfully reduced peak river flow and protected buildings. It then identifies additional environmental benefits of the methods used: improving water quality, preventing erosion and, in some cases, storing carbon.

These effects are separate from the immediate reduction of flooding. Therefore, the evidence establishes that natural flood management can provide benefits beyond flood prevention. This is the conclusion expressed in B.

items.label: A
items.text: The passage reports that the scheme reduced flood risk in one case but provides no evidence about its effectiveness under exceptionally heavy rainfall.

items.label: C
items.text: The reduction in floodwater was attributed approximately equally to upstream land management and flood storage, but this does not establish that every natural flood management method is equally effective.

items.label: D
items.text: The success of one scheme does not establish that natural flood management is suitable or necessary in every flood-prone location.

items.label: E
items.text: The described scheme involved hills and upstream land management, but the passage provides no comparison with schemes in other landscapes to establish where these methods are most effective.

Despite the recent decline in numbers of people getting married, it appears that there is still much to recommend it. Married people are happier, wealthier and live longer. Husbands and wives have a lower risk of disease and a higher life expectancy. They smoke less, drink less and eat more healthily. Those who get married and stay married have on average double the amount of wealth of those who never marry. Surveys show that they are happier than single people and less likely to experience mid-life depression. Married couples benefit from stronger networks of support, with relatives providing more care and assistance in old age and in times of need. Finding and committing to a marriage partner is a goal well worth pursuing.
Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above reasoning?

Husbands and wives have a lower risk of disease and a higher life expectancy. They smoke less, drink less and eat more healthily. Those who get married and stay married have on average double the amount of wealth of those who never marry. Surveys show that they are happier than single people and less likely to experience mid-life depression. Married couples benefit from stronger networks of support, with relatives providing more care and assistance in old age and in times of need. Finding and committing to a marriage partner is a goal well worth pursuing.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above reasoning?

options.label: A
options.text: Research suggests that being married boosts the chances of surviving cancer.

options.label: B
options.text: Statistics on marriage do not differentiate between those who have children and those who do not.

options.label: C
options.text: In many countries, being married gives advantages in terms of tax payments.

options.label: D
options.text: Individuals in conflict-ridden relationships are more prone to illness than happy couples.

options.label: E
options.text: Wealthier couples are four times more likely to marry than poorer couples.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument uses the observation that married people tend to be wealthier, healthier and happier to recommend pursuing marriage. This reasoning assumes that marriage itself contributes to these advantages rather than merely being associated with them.

E weakens this inference by stating that wealthier couples are four times more likely to marry than poorer couples. This suggests an alternative explanation for married people's greater average wealth: people who are already financially better off may be more likely to get married. Therefore, the observed association between marriage and wealth does not necessarily show that marriage produces greater wealth. This weakens an important part of the argument supporting marriage.

items.label: A
items.text: Evidence that marriage improves cancer survival would support the claim that marriage contributes to better health outcomes.

items.label: B
items.text: Differences in whether married people have children might complicate the statistics, but the option does not establish that parenthood explains the reported advantages.

items.label: C
items.text: Tax advantages for married couples could help explain why marriage contributes to greater wealth. This supports rather than undermines the claimed financial benefits.

items.label: D
items.text: Conflict-ridden relationships may be associated with poorer health, showing that relationship quality matters. However, this does not directly challenge the claim about married people's average advantages as strongly as the selection effect identified in E.

Three friends are training to run a marathon. Part of this training involves running steadily round a track in the local park. They are all at different stages in their training schedules so they run at different speeds. Alec completes each lap in 3 minutes, Barry takes 5 minutes and Colin takes 6 minutes.
They all leave the start line at the same time.
If they each maintain their running speed throughout the session, how many more laps will Alec have completed compared to Barry when the three of them next cross the start line together?

main_body.text:
Three friends are training to run a marathon. Part of this training involves running steadily round a track in the local park. They are all at different stages in their training schedules so they run at different speeds. Alec completes each lap in 3 minutes, Barry takes 5 minutes and Colin takes 6 minutes.
They all leave the start line at the same time.

question_view.main_question: If they each maintain their running speed throughout the session, how many more laps will Alec have completed compared to Barry when the three of them next cross the start line together?

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The three runners complete one lap every 3, 5 and 6 minutes respectively. For all three to cross the start line simultaneously again, the elapsed time must be a common multiple of all three lap times.

The lowest common multiple of 3, 5 and 6 is 30 minutes. In that time, Alec completes 30 ÷ 3 = 10 laps, while Barry completes 30 ÷ 5 = 6 laps.

The difference is 10 − 6 = 4 laps. Therefore, B is correct.

items.label: A
items.text: 2 laps is below the calculated difference of 4 at the first time all three runners return to the start line together.

items.label: C
items.text: 5 laps exceeds the difference between Alec's 10 completed laps and Barry's 6 completed laps by one.

items.label: D
items.text: 6 is the number of laps Barry completes in 30 minutes, not the number of additional laps completed by Alec.

items.label: E
items.text: 10 is Alec's total number of completed laps at the next simultaneous crossing, not his lead over Barry.

main_body.text:
It is universally recognised that Africa’s conservation tourism provides employment, generates wealth and educates future generations while saving endangered species. So we should champion tourism for the sake of conservation. Tourism in the Arctic is thus to be welcomed.
As the Arctic ice melts, new shipping routes are opening up. It is unfair to characterise the presence of a large cruise ship in the Northwest Passage as ‘extinction tourism’ that merely indulges people who want to view endangered animals before it is too late. The tourists will return home better informed about the Arctic’s fragile ecosystem.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the flaw in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: It argues a general rule on the basis of one successful example of wildlife tourism.

options.label: B
options.text: It assumes that wildlife tourists only want to see endangered animals.

options.label: C
options.text: It assumes that wildlife tourism is more important than successful conservation.

options.label: D
options.text: It assumes that the cruise-ship tourists will see enough to return home committed to the conservation of the Arctic ecosystem.

options.label: E
options.text: The argument implies that conservation tourism will inevitably lead to the extinction of some species of animal.

blocks.text: The argument uses the success of conservation tourism in Africa to justify welcoming tourism in the Arctic. However, evidence that tourism generates wealth, employment and conservation benefits in one region does not establish that it will produce comparable benefits elsewhere. The Arctic may face different conditions, and the passage provides no evidence that cruise tourism there will protect endangered species or support conservation as African tourism allegedly does. Therefore, A identifies the flaw: generalising from one successful example of wildlife tourism to tourism in other environments.

items.label: B
items.text: The argument explicitly challenges the claim that tourists merely want to see endangered animals, suggesting that they may also gain knowledge. It does not assume that viewing animals is their only motivation.

items.label: C
items.text: The argument presents tourism as beneficial because it supports conservation. It does not treat tourism as more important than successful conservation.

items.label: D
items.text: The passage predicts that tourists will return better informed, but it does not require them to become committed conservationists. Its broader weakness is extending the African example to the Arctic.

items.label: E
items.text: The argument presents conservation tourism as helping endangered species survive, not as inevitably causing their extinction.
