question_view.main_question: Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: If the snake that bit this woman was a king cobra, then she would be dead by now. As she is alive and well, the snake can’t have been a king cobra.

options.label: B
options.text: If the snake had yellow markings, then it was a pit viper. You say it did have yellow markings, so it must have been a pit viper.

options.label: C
options.text:
If what Mahmood saw was a diamondback rattlesnake, he would have been in real danger.
Since there are no rattlesnakes where Mahmood was, he was actually quite safe.

options.label: D
options.text: If a snake bite goes untreated for too long, there can be serious complications. Since I got prompt treatment, I didn’t have any complications.

options.label: E
options.text: If the snake that bit this victim was venomous, then the wound would be very inflamed. We can see that there is severe inflammation, so the snake must have been venomous.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The original argument states that unlawful conduct would require the vice president to resign. It then observes that he has resigned and concludes that he must have acted unlawfully. This incorrectly treats a consequence as proof of its proposed cause: resignation could occur for reasons other than unlawful conduct.

E follows the same pattern. It states that a venomous snake bite would cause severe inflammation, then concludes that the snake must have been venomous because inflammation is present. Both arguments affirm the consequent: if P then Q; Q occurs; therefore P. This inference is invalid because Q may have other causes.

items.label: A
items.text: This applies the contrapositive: if a king cobra bite guarantees death, survival rules out a king cobra bite. It does not infer a cause from the presence of its consequence.

items.label: B
items.text: Yellow markings are presented as sufficient evidence of a pit viper, and the conclusion applies that condition directly. This is not the same reversed inference.

items.label: C
items.text: The argument rules out the stated rattlesnake danger because rattlesnakes are absent, rather than inferring the original cause from an observed consequence.

items.label: D
items.text: This reasons from receiving prompt treatment to the absence of complications, although the original conditional only concerns delayed treatment. It denies the antecedent rather than affirming the consequent.

question_view.question_text:
It’s common for people to agree in principle to socially useful projects such as the opening of centres for people with serious mental health problems. However, if the project is planned for the area where they live, they tend to object and suggest that alternative locations would be preferable. While they approve of the general idea of such projects, they won’t tolerate any negative effects on their own lives. We really don’t want to go back to outdated practices of housing people with mental health problems in remote areas with no contact with the general population. So we have to accept that these projects can only work if we live near, and interact with, the people they are designed to help. Practise what you preach!
Which one of the following illustrates the principle used in the above argument?

main_body.text: It’s common for people to agree in principle to socially useful projects such as the opening of centres for people with serious mental health problems. However, if the project is planned for the area where they live, they tend to object and suggest that alternative locations would be preferable. While they approve of the general idea of such projects, they won’t tolerate any negative effects on their own lives. We really don’t want to go back to outdated practices of housing people with mental health problems in remote areas with no contact with the general population. So we have to accept that these projects can only work if we live near, and interact with, the people they are designed to help. Practise what you preach!

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following illustrates the principle used in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: People who think sport has been tainted by bribery and performance-enhancing drugs should not buy tickets to sporting events.

options.label: B
options.text: People who think more money should be spent on the health service should not complain when their income tax is increased to fund it.

options.label: C
options.text: Parents who think too much ‘screen time’ is bad for young children should not buy them so many electronic gadgets.

options.label: D
options.text: People who choose to be vegetarians should seek to persuade others not to eat meat or fish.

options.label: E
options.text: People who have benefitted from grants or bursaries for university education should lobby for others to have the same advantages.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument establishes that people who support socially beneficial projects must be willing to accept the personal inconvenience or cost necessary for those projects to succeed. Supporting a mental health centre in principle while refusing to live near its users is inconsistent because integration into ordinary communities is essential to the proposed approach.

B illustrates the same principle. People who support increased healthcare funding should accept the higher taxes required to finance it rather than supporting the benefit while objecting to their personal contribution. Both arguments require consistency between endorsing a collective benefit and accepting its individual costs.

items.label: A
items.text: Refusing to support sporting events because of corruption concerns expresses consistency between criticism and consumer behaviour, but it does not specifically concern accepting a personal cost necessary to provide a public benefit.

items.label: C
items.text: Parents limiting their children's access to gadgets would make their actions consistent with their beliefs, but the issue concerns private parenting choices rather than sharing the burdens of a socially beneficial project.

items.label: D
items.text: Vegetarians encouraging others to adopt their diet extends a personal conviction to other people. It does not require them to accept personal disadvantages associated with a collective policy they support.

items.label: E
items.text: Supporting access to benefits previously received by oneself concerns extending opportunities to others, not accepting the personal costs of implementing a publicly supported project.

People are quick to connect attempts to reduce the effects of climate change with the protection of the environment. However, responding to climate change is much more important for humanity than for nature. In the history of the planet, the relative stability of temperatures in the last ten thousand years is the exception rather than the norm. Nature has always found a way to adapt to large temperature variations but human civilisations, all of which have evolved in the last ten thousand years, have developed in a period with unusually reliable and predictable weather. Nature will find a way to move on, but climate change is potentially devastating for humans.
Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

Chiropractors rely heavily on manipulating their patients’ spines. This has benefits for some patients, but more than half of all patients suffer mild to moderate adverse effects after seeing a chiropractor. These are mostly local and referred pains that usually last for two to three days.
Chiropractors often claim that these are necessary steps on the road to getting better.
However, several hundred cases have been documented in which patients were seriously and often permanently damaged after chiropractic manipulations. What usually happens in these tragic instances is that, upon manipulation of the upper spine, an artery supplying the brain is overstretched and simply breaks up, leading to a stroke that can prove fatal.
Which one of the following is a conclusion that can be drawn from the above passage?

main_body.text:
Chiropractors rely heavily on manipulating their patients’ spines. This has benefits for some patients, but more than half of all patients suffer mild to moderate adverse effects after seeing a chiropractor. These are mostly local and referred pains that usually last for two to three days.
Chiropractors often claim that these are necessary steps on the road to getting better.
However, several hundred cases have been documented in which patients were seriously and often permanently damaged after chiropractic manipulations. What usually happens in these tragic instances is that, upon manipulation of the upper spine, an artery supplying the brain is overstretched and simply breaks up, leading to a stroke that can prove fatal.

options.label: B
options.text: Chiropractic therapy may do more harm than good.

options.label: C
options.text: The spine is the most delicate part of the human body.

options.label: D

blocks.text:

These risks establish that chiropractic treatment can produce harm, sometimes severe, despite its possible benefits. The evidence therefore supports the cautious conclusion that chiropractic therapy may do more harm than good, as stated in B. It does not establish that harm necessarily outweighs benefits in every case.

items.text: The reported risks raise safety concerns, but the passage also acknowledges benefits for some patients. It does not establish that banning all chiropractic treatment is necessary.

items.text: Consulting a doctor beforehand might be a precaution, but the passage provides no evidence that doing so would prevent the described injuries.

items.label: E

question_view.question_text:
Drivers found to be committing offences such as speeding are now offered the choice between paying the police for a re-education course or taking the traditional penalty of paying a fine and receiving penalty points on their licence. It is no surprise that the number of motorists opting for re-education courses has tripled in five years, but the high cost of such courses has led to accusations that police forces might use the new system for their own benefit. They could easily set up speed traps, catch a number of motorists slightly over the limit, and generate easy income for themselves. Re-education courses are a good idea in theory, but open to abuse by cash-starved police forces.
Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

main_body.text: Drivers found to be committing offences such as speeding are now offered the choice between paying the police for a re-education course or taking the traditional penalty of paying a fine and receiving penalty points on their licence. It is no surprise that the number of motorists opting for re-education courses has tripled in five years, but the high cost of such courses has led to accusations that police forces might use the new system for their own benefit. They could easily set up speed traps, catch a number of motorists slightly over the limit, and generate easy income for themselves. Re-education courses are a good idea in theory, but open to abuse by cash-starved police forces.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The cost of running re-education courses is less than the combined contributions of participants.

options.label: B
options.text: Re-education is more effective than punishment in preventing further motoring offences.

options.label: C
options.text: Police forces are more interested in generating income than in preventing motoring offences.

options.label: D
options.text: The number of driving offences committed in the last five years has tripled.

options.label: E
options.text: Fear of losing a driving licence is greater than fear of financial hardship.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument warns that police forces might exploit re-education courses to generate income by catching motorists committing relatively minor offences and collecting course fees. For this proposed financial incentive to exist, the money collected from participants must exceed the cost of providing the courses.

If the courses cost as much as or more than the fees collected, increasing participation would not generate the surplus revenue described. Therefore, A is the underlying assumption necessary for the argument that police forces could benefit financially from expanding the scheme.

items.label: B
items.text: The concern is that police might exploit courses for revenue, not that re-education prevents offences more effectively than conventional penalties.

items.label: C
items.text: The argument suggests that financial pressure could create incentives for abuse. It does not require police forces to be generally more interested in income than road safety.

items.label: D
items.text: The number of people choosing courses has tripled, but this does not establish that the total number of driving offences has tripled. The financial concern does not require such an increase.

items.label: E
items.text: Drivers' preferences between penalty points and financial costs might affect their choices, but the argument about police revenue does not depend on one fear being greater than the other.

question_view.question_text:
A band of rebellious traders in Wales has decided to take their whole town ‘offshore’ in protest at the insignificant amounts of UK tax paid by big businesses. An alliance of shopkeepers from the town want to use the same controversial loopholes favoured by huge multinationals such as Google so that they too can legally avoid UK tax. The coffee giant Starbucks, for example, has been branded immoral for transferring revenues out of the UK and into the Netherlands and Switzerland, where they receive sweetened tax deals. But the shopkeepers of the town cannot have it both ways. If they believe it is immoral for Starbucks to avoid UK tax, it is immoral for them, too. They should continue to pay UK tax in full.
Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

main_body.text: A band of rebellious traders in Wales has decided to take their whole town ‘offshore’ in protest at the insignificant amounts of UK tax paid by big businesses. An alliance of shopkeepers from the town want to use the same controversial loopholes favoured by huge multinationals such as Google so that they too can legally avoid UK tax. The coffee giant Starbucks, for example, has been branded immoral for transferring revenues out of the UK and into the Netherlands and Switzerland, where they receive sweetened tax deals. But the shopkeepers of the town cannot have it both ways. If they believe it is immoral for Starbucks to avoid UK tax, it is immoral for them, too. They should continue to pay UK tax in full.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The sole purpose of the protest is to pressure the government into tackling tax avoidance by big business.

options.label: C
options.text: Small businesses acting alone cannot obtain the same tax breaks as the giant corporations.

options.label: D
options.text: Every time the government comes up with a way of tackling tax avoidance, lawyers simply find a new loophole.

blocks.text:
The argument claims that Welsh shopkeepers would be acting inconsistently if they avoided UK taxes while condemning large corporations for doing the same. It therefore concludes that the shopkeepers should continue paying their taxes in full.

A weakens this criticism by explaining that the shopkeepers' sole purpose is to pressure the government into tackling corporate tax avoidance. Their proposed actions would then be a form of protest against the system rather than an attempt to gain the same financial advantages they condemn. This difference in purpose provides a reason to distinguish the morality of their protest from the corporations' tax-avoidance practices.

items.label: B
items.text: If similar protests harmed the economy, this would provide an additional reason to oppose the shopkeepers' actions rather than weaken the argument against them.

items.label: C
items.text: Small businesses being unable to obtain the same tax benefits would question the feasibility of the proposed scheme, but it would not undermine the principle that comparable tax avoidance should be judged consistently.

items.label: D
items.text: The existence of continually emerging loopholes explains difficulties in addressing tax avoidance but does not establish that shopkeepers are morally justified in using those loopholes.

items.label: E
items.text: The difference between one trader's taxes and Facebook's taxes may explain the protest, but unequal payments alone do not establish that avoiding taxes is morally acceptable for the trader.

Although using a smartphone or other mobile phone behind the wheel of a car is most certainly dangerous, research is showing that very frequent usage of the phones is harmful more generally. A study has found that individuals with relatively high levels of mobile phone usage are more likely to demonstrate cognitive failures, which can range from forgetting appointments to accidentally bumping into things in the environment. Cognitive failures are associated with the short attention spans also observed in high-frequency mobile phone users.
Clearly, if people want to reduce their risk of cognitive failures, they should limit the amount of time they spend on their mobile phones.
Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

main_body.text:
Much concern is paid to the hazards posed by people using mobile phones while operating motor vehicles. Although using a smartphone or other mobile phone behind the wheel of a car is most certainly dangerous, research is showing that very frequent usage of the phones is harmful more generally. A study has found that individuals with relatively high levels of mobile phone usage are more likely to demonstrate cognitive failures, which can range from forgetting appointments to accidentally bumping into things in the environment. Cognitive failures are associated with the short attention spans also observed in high-frequency mobile phone users.
Clearly, if people want to reduce their risk of cognitive failures, they should limit the amount of time they spend on their mobile phones.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: High-frequency mobile phone users may have had short attention spans prior to the formation of their phone usage habits.

options.label: B
options.text: Limiting one’s smartphone or mobile phone usage may not be a sufficient strategy for significantly reducing cognitive failures.

options.label: C
options.text: Mobile phones may play an important role in the completion of everyday tasks in the lives of many people.

options.label: D
options.text: Smartphones and other mobile phones may have different applications or features that are not all used in the exact same fashion.

options.label: E
options.text: The risks posed by using a mobile phone while driving may be much greater than those posed by too-frequent usage of the phones overall.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument observes that frequent mobile phone users are more likely to experience cognitive failures and short attention spans. It then concludes that reducing phone use will lower the risk of these problems.

However, this assumes that frequent phone use causes the observed cognitive difficulties. A identifies an alternative explanation: individuals might already have short attention spans before developing their phone habits. Such people could be more inclined to use phones frequently, meaning their pre-existing characteristics help explain the association. If so, reducing phone use might not resolve the underlying cause. Therefore, A identifies the causal flaw.

items.label: B
items.text: The argument recommends limiting phone use to reduce risk, not eliminating every cognitive failure. A strategy need not be sufficient on its own to produce some reduction in risk.

items.label: C
items.text: Phones may provide practical benefits in everyday life, but those benefits do not establish whether frequent usage causes cognitive problems.

items.label: D
items.text: Different phone functions may involve different activities, but the option does not identify an alternative cause of the observed association between frequent use and cognitive failures.

items.label: E
items.text: The relative danger of phone use while driving concerns a different risk. It does not determine whether general phone use causes the cognitive difficulties described.

question_view.question_text:
Nearly everyone thinks it is a bad thing to be a hypocrite, because it is profoundly dishonest to pretend to have moral standards that you do not actually have. But pretending you are better than you are is evidence that you still accept the moral principles you have failed to follow. So it is better than being shameless about your moral failings. Perceived in this way, hypocrisy can be considered to be a virtue. Being a hypocrite shows you feel a need to hide some aspect of your life because it would be too embarrassing to allow it into the open. Many hypocrites wish they were the people they pretend to be: so perhaps one day they will succeed.
Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

main_body.text: Nearly everyone thinks it is a bad thing to be a hypocrite, because it is profoundly dishonest to pretend to have moral standards that you do not actually have. But pretending you are better than you are is evidence that you still accept the moral principles you have failed to follow. So it is better than being shameless about your moral failings. Perceived in this way, hypocrisy can be considered to be a virtue. Being a hypocrite shows you feel a need to hide some aspect of your life because it would be too embarrassing to allow it into the open. Many hypocrites wish they were the people they pretend to be: so perhaps one day they will succeed.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Hypocrisy is evidence of an inner need to conceal a shameful aspect of one’s life.

options.label: B
options.text: It is bad not to show any shame for the mistakes one makes in life.

options.label: C
options.text: In some cases, hypocrisy may lead to moral improvement.

options.label: D
options.text: It is possible to think of hypocrisy as a good thing.

options.label: E
options.text: Hypocrisy is a serious moral weakness.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument challenges the conventional judgement that hypocrisy is necessarily bad. Although hypocrites fail to follow the moral standards they profess, their desire to appear morally better suggests that they still recognise those standards as desirable.

This distinguishes hypocrisy from openly disregarding moral principles. The passage also suggests that some hypocrites genuinely aspire to become the people they pretend to be, potentially leading to improvement. These considerations support the author's central conclusion that hypocrisy can sometimes be regarded as a virtue rather than exclusively as a moral failing. Therefore, D is correct.

items.label: A
items.text: The desire to conceal embarrassing behaviour is presented as evidence that hypocrites recognise moral standards. It supports the conclusion rather than expressing the broader judgement about hypocrisy.

items.label: B
items.text: The criticism of shamelessness helps explain why hypocrisy might be preferable to openly disregarding morality, but it is not the main conclusion.

items.label: C
items.text: The possibility of future moral improvement is one reason for evaluating hypocrisy more positively. The conclusion is broader than this potential consequence.

items.label: E
items.text: This reflects the conventional negative view of hypocrisy that the author explicitly challenges by presenting reasons for a more favourable interpretation.

question_view.question_text:
One of the greatest achievements of English grammar schools was the development and dissemination of a sophisticated system of standard punctuation for the English language. The complex rules for the use of commas conveyed a range of precise meanings, while the choice between semi-colon, colon and full stop expressed the exact, and often subtle, relationship between statements. Without this kind of attention to punctuation, there is bound to be a loss of precision in communication and in thinking. The current use of commas to join statements together, without any regard for grammar or the nature of the link between them, lacks rigour and covers up lazy thinking.
Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above?

main_body.text: One of the greatest achievements of English grammar schools was the development and dissemination of a sophisticated system of standard punctuation for the English language. The complex rules for the use of commas conveyed a range of precise meanings, while the choice between semi-colon, colon and full stop expressed the exact, and often subtle, relationship between statements. Without this kind of attention to punctuation, there is bound to be a loss of precision in communication and in thinking. The current use of commas to join statements together, without any regard for grammar or the nature of the link between them, lacks rigour and covers up lazy thinking.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above?

options.label: A
options.text: Most writers do not want to waste time thinking through the exact connections between their ideas.

options.label: B
options.text: Only a minority of people ever grasped the finer aspects of the traditional system of punctuation.

options.label: C
options.text: Schools should go back to teaching the traditional system of punctuation.

options.label: D
options.text: The government should reintroduce grammar schools into the UK.

options.label: E
options.text: The vocabulary and grammar of a language naturally evolve over time, and the same is true of punctuation.

blocks.text:
The passage argues that traditional punctuation rules enabled writers to communicate precise relationships between ideas. Commas, semicolons, colons and full stops served different functions, allowing subtle distinctions in meaning.

The author criticises contemporary punctuation practices for disregarding these distinctions, thereby reducing precision in communication and encouraging imprecise thinking. Since traditional punctuation is presented as providing valuable clarity that current practices often lack, the passage supports restoring its instruction in schools. Therefore, C is the conclusion that can be drawn.

items.label: B
items.text: The author praises the traditional system's precision but provides no evidence about how many people successfully mastered its finer rules.

items.label: D

question_view.question_text:
Long hours and poor pay have become commonly accepted, but they are taking a heavy toll on life at home. It is not a pretty picture: an economy where high levels of stress and anxiety are normal, where people get ill because they have lost control of their time, and where marriages are damaged and children suffer. Yet it is a situation that politicians invite us to applaud. They praise ‘strivers’ and ‘hard-working people’, not chilled-out, caring mums and dads. The longer and harder we work, the more admirable we are supposed to be. So the political slogans have clearly been effective, but the resulting glorification of work has made us miserable.
Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

main_body.text: Long hours and poor pay have become commonly accepted, but they are taking a heavy toll on life at home. It is not a pretty picture: an economy where high levels of stress and anxiety are normal, where people get ill because they have lost control of their time, and where marriages are damaged and children suffer. Yet it is a situation that politicians invite us to applaud. They praise ‘strivers’ and ‘hard-working people’, not chilled-out, caring mums and dads. The longer and harder we work, the more admirable we are supposed to be. So the political slogans have clearly been effective, but the resulting glorification of work has made us miserable.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Most employees are not satisfied with their salary.

options.label: B
options.text: Political slogans significantly affect people’s everyday behaviour.

options.label: C
options.text: Restructuring the working week would be beneficial for the economy.

options.label: D
options.text: Companies could afford shorter hours or better pay for their employees.

options.label: E
options.text: People who experience less stress at work are better parents.

blocks.text:
The argument claims that politicians praise relentless work and present longer hours as evidence of admirable character. It then concludes that these political messages have successfully encouraged the glorification of work, contributing to stress, damaged relationships and unhappiness.

For political slogans to be responsible for this outcome, they must meaningfully influence how people behave or what working habits they adopt. If slogans had no significant effect on everyday behaviour, the argument could not attribute the harmful work culture to their success. Therefore, B is the underlying assumption.

items.label: C
items.text: The argument criticises the social consequences of overwork but does not require restructuring the working week to benefit economic performance.

items.label: D
items.text: Whether employers could afford shorter hours or higher wages concerns possible solutions, not the assumed influence of political rhetoric on working habits.

items.label: E
items.text: Stress may affect family relationships, but the argument does not require a general comparison establishing that less-stressed workers are better parents.

question_view.question_text:
Despite recent improvements to their training, a new study suggests that the police are as susceptible as the general public to holding false beliefs about crime and punishment.
Participants in the study were questioned about their views on a number of crime-related myths such as ‘capital punishment is an effective way to deter criminal activity’ – myths, because they are unsupported by research evidence. Police were just as likely to endorse the misconceptions as the lay participants and, moreover, were more confident in their false beliefs. This is a worrying example of a ‘scientist–practitioner gap’, a term which describes a situation where professionals do not accept the evidence of research relevant to their roles.
Studies have shown that training can permanently reduce the ‘scientist–practitioner gap’. Police officers need more training.
Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?

main_body.text:
Despite recent improvements to their training, a new study suggests that the police are as susceptible as the general public to holding false beliefs about crime and punishment.
Participants in the study were questioned about their views on a number of crime-related myths such as ‘capital punishment is an effective way to deter criminal activity’ – myths, because they are unsupported by research evidence. Police were just as likely to endorse the misconceptions as the lay participants and, moreover, were more confident in their false beliefs. This is a worrying example of a ‘scientist–practitioner gap’, a term which describes a situation where professionals do not accept the evidence of research relevant to their roles.
Studies have shown that training can permanently reduce the ‘scientist–practitioner gap’. Police officers need more training.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The recruitment process for new police officers often fails to identify false beliefs held by applicants.

options.label: B
options.text: The majority of police officers do not support the return of capital punishment.

options.label: C
options.text: The science–practitioner gap is a common phenomenon in many professions, not just the police.

options.label: D
options.text: Police training has often been criticised in the media for being insufficiently practical.

options.label: E
options.text: Police officers whose views are not evidence-based are more likely to have complaints made against them by members of the public.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument identifies a gap between research evidence and police officers' beliefs about crime and punishment. Officers are reported to endorse unsupported misconceptions and to express considerable confidence in those beliefs. It then recommends additional training because research indicates that training can reduce this scientist–practitioner gap.

E strengthens the recommendation by establishing that officers whose views are not evidence-based are more likely to receive public complaints. This connects the identified problem with adverse professional consequences, providing an additional practical reason to address misconceptions through training.

items.label: A
items.text: Recruitment failing to identify misconceptions suggests another source of the problem, but it does not directly establish that officers' existing false beliefs have harmful consequences or that additional training is especially important.

items.label: B
items.text: Opposition to capital punishment does not establish that officers avoid other crime-related misconceptions. It offers little support for the recommendation.

items.label: C
items.text: The existence of similar gaps in other professions shows that the problem is widespread, but it does not establish the consequences of such beliefs among police officers.

items.label: D
items.text: Criticism that training is insufficiently practical concerns the character of existing programmes, not specifically whether additional evidence-based training would correct misconceptions.

question_view.question_text:
An accident at the Fukushima nuclear power plant in Japan in 2011 caused the release of radioactive material, resulting in around half a million people being evacuated from the area.
These people have not been allowed to return to the area because of the health risks of exposure to radiation. But the psychological consequences of long-term evacuation may be more significant than the physical effects of radiation. People who wish to return to live in the area around Fukushima should be allowed to. Studies of a similar situation at Chernobyl showed that average life expectancy for evacuees reduced – not predominantly because of cancer caused by radiation, but because of depression, alcoholism and suicide due to the impact of permanent evacuation. There is, moreover, massive disagreement in the scientific community over how much radiation is ‘safe’.
Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

main_body.text:
An accident at the Fukushima nuclear power plant in Japan in 2011 caused the release of radioactive material, resulting in around half a million people being evacuated from the area.
These people have not been allowed to return to the area because of the health risks of exposure to radiation. But the psychological consequences of long-term evacuation may be more significant than the physical effects of radiation. People who wish to return to live in the area around Fukushima should be allowed to. Studies of a similar situation at Chernobyl showed that average life expectancy for evacuees reduced – not predominantly because of cancer caused by radiation, but because of depression, alcoholism and suicide due to the impact of permanent evacuation. There is, moreover, massive disagreement in the scientific community over how much radiation is ‘safe’.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The increased risks of cancer due to exposure to radiation have been exaggerated.

options.label: B
options.text: There is no consensus among scientists about what constitutes a safe level of radiation.

options.label: C
options.text: People who are forcibly evacuated from their homes experience reduced life expectancy.

options.label: D
options.text: People should be allowed to make their own decisions about living in the affected area.

options.label: E
options.text: The negative effects of radiation may be less significant than the psychological consequences of evacuation.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument contrasts the physical risks of radiation exposure with the psychological consequences of prolonged compulsory evacuation. Evidence from Chernobyl suggests that evacuation-related depression, alcoholism and suicide contributed substantially to reduced life expectancy. The passage also notes scientific disagreement over safe radiation levels.

Together, these considerations support allowing affected individuals to weigh the uncertain physical risks against the potential psychological harm of remaining displaced. The main conclusion is therefore that people wishing to return to the Fukushima area should be permitted to make that decision themselves, as stated in D.

items.label: A
items.text: The passage questions whether evacuation-related harms may outweigh radiation risks, but it does not establish that cancer risks themselves have been exaggerated.

items.label: B
items.text: Scientific disagreement about safe radiation levels is explicitly presented as evidence supporting individual choice. It is not the main policy conclusion.

items.label: C
items.text: Reduced life expectancy among Chernobyl evacuees is cited as supporting evidence. The passage does not establish that every forced evacuation produces this outcome.

items.label: E
items.text: The possibility that psychological consequences exceed radiation-related harms is a central reason for permitting individuals to return, but it is not the final recommendation.

question_view.question_text:
Your cake will be tasty only if you use fresh ingredients which you can only buy at the market.
You did not go to the market, so your cake will not be tasty.
Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

main_body.text:
Your cake will be tasty only if you use fresh ingredients which you can only buy at the market.
You did not go to the market, so your cake will not be tasty.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: You can only be happy if you are healthy. To be healthy, you have to eat a lot of vegetables. You eat a lot of vegetables so you must be happy.

options.label: B
options.text: She either went to school or to the playground. She is not in the playground, so she must have gone to school.

options.label: C
options.text: If you light a candle, there is light and, if there is light, I am able to read to you. You must have lit a candle because I can read.

options.label: D
options.text: Listening to loud music through earphones damages hearing. His hearing is fine which means that he must not have listened to loud music through earphones.

options.label: E
options.text: Good knowledge of the car is necessary for fixing it. Without fixing the car, we will not arrive at the wedding in time. We will surely be late as we do not have good knowledge of the car.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The original argument establishes two necessary conditions: a tasty cake requires fresh ingredients, and obtaining those ingredients requires visiting the market. Therefore, if the market was not visited, the necessary ingredients could not have been obtained, so the cake cannot be tasty.

E follows the same chain. Fixing the car requires good knowledge of it, and arriving at the wedding on time requires fixing the car. Without the necessary knowledge, the car cannot be fixed, and without fixing it, timely arrival is impossible. Both arguments use the absence of a necessary condition to rule out a later outcome.

items.label: A
items.text: Health and vegetable consumption are presented as necessary conditions for happiness, but the conclusion treats eating vegetables as sufficient to guarantee happiness. This reverses the conditional reasoning.

items.label: B
items.text: The argument eliminates one of two alternative destinations and infers the other. It does not follow a chain of necessary conditions.

items.label: C
items.text: The argument infers that a candle was lit because reading is possible, although other sources of light could permit reading. It affirms the consequent instead of eliminating an outcome through an absent necessary condition.

items.label: D
items.text: The argument uses the absence of hearing damage to rule out loud music through earphones. This is a single contrapositive rather than the linked necessary conditions in the original argument.

question_view.question_text:
Costs of health care in the UK are shared through taxation, but some of those who can afford to pay for a higher standard of care choose to do so. Some think it is immoral for rich people to receive better health care simply because they can afford to pay for it. But the whole point of money is to enable those who have it to improve the quality of life of themselves and their families. If money did not offer such advantages, it would not motivate people to develop their skills or to work harder in order to earn more. Since people are morally entitled to use their money to buy advantages for themselves and their loved ones, there can be no objection to private medicine.
Which one of the following illustrates the principle used in the above argument?

main_body.text: Costs of health care in the UK are shared through taxation, but some of those who can afford to pay for a higher standard of care choose to do so. Some think it is immoral for rich people to receive better health care simply because they can afford to pay for it. But the whole point of money is to enable those who have it to improve the quality of life of themselves and their families. If money did not offer such advantages, it would not motivate people to develop their skills or to work harder in order to earn more. Since people are morally entitled to use their money to buy advantages for themselves and their loved ones, there can be no objection to private medicine.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following illustrates the principle used in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: People who have been born rich should not waste their inherited wealth in gambling, self-indulgence and extravagant living.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a good thing for people from rich countries to take foreign holidays, because the income generated by tourism benefits the local economy.

options.label: C
options.text: People who are born talented are under a moral obligation to develop their talents and to apply them energetically for the good of humanity.

options.label: D
options.text: Rich people should give away some of their wealth to benefit those less fortunate than themselves.

options.label: E
options.text: Inheritance tax should be set at a fairly low rate so that the children of rich parents inherit enough money to make a substantial difference to their lives.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The argument defends private healthcare on the principle that people are morally entitled to use their money to improve their own lives and those of their families. The ability to purchase advantages is presented as a legitimate purpose of wealth, even when those advantages are not equally available to everyone.

E applies the same principle to inheritance: low inheritance taxes would allow wealthy parents to pass on enough money to materially improve their children's lives. Both arguments defend using personal wealth to provide advantages for family members, rather than requiring those advantages to be equally accessible to all.

items.label: A
items.text: This restricts how wealthy individuals should spend inherited money, whereas the original principle defends their entitlement to use wealth to improve their own and their families' lives.

items.label: B
items.text: Foreign holidays are defended because they benefit local economies, not because individuals are entitled to purchase personal advantages with their money.

items.label: C
items.text: This imposes a duty to use natural talents for society's benefit. The original argument instead defends the individual's right to use earned resources for personal and family benefits.

items.label: D
items.text: This recommends redistributing wealth to less fortunate people. The original principle specifically defends wealthy individuals using their resources to benefit themselves and their loved ones.

question_view.question_text:
Sourdough, an ingredient of many bread products, is a fermented mixture of flour and water. At
8:00am on Monday morning, I start with a mixture of 50g flour and 50g water. Each morning at
8:00am I double the weight of the sourdough by adding equal weights of flour and water.
I know that 1g of the water content evaporates every hour.
The bread recipe that I would like to use requires 500g of sourdough. I also want at least 50g of sourdough left over so that I can continue growing it for next week’s bread.
On which day am I going to have the necessary amount of sourdough?

main_body.text:
Sourdough, an ingredient of many bread products, is a fermented mixture of flour and water. At
8:00am on Monday morning, I start with a mixture of 50g flour and 50g water. Each morning at
8:00am I double the weight of the sourdough by adding equal weights of flour and water.
I know that 1g of the water content evaporates every hour.
The bread recipe that I would like to use requires 500g of sourdough. I also want at least 50g of sourdough left over so that I can continue growing it for next week’s bread.

question_view.main_question: On which day am I going to have the necessary amount of sourdough?

options.label: A
options.text: Tuesday

options.label: B
options.text: Wednesday

options.label: C
options.text: Thursday

options.label: D
options.text: Friday

options.label: E
options.text: Saturday

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The baker needs 500g for the recipe and at least 50g remaining, so the total sourdough required is 550g. The mixture initially weighs 100g on Monday morning. It loses 1g of water per hour, or 24g between daily additions. Each morning, its remaining weight is doubled by adding equal weights of flour and water.

Tuesday: (100 − 24) × 2 = 152g.
Wednesday: (152 − 24) × 2 = 256g.
Thursday: (256 − 24) × 2 = 464g.
Friday: (464 − 24) × 2 = 880g.

question_view.question_text:
The 21st century is witnessing a significant rise in the proportion of people being diagnosed by medical professionals as having a mental illness. For example, at the turn of the century, the number of Canadians being treated for depression increased by over 30% in just one year. A recent study in the US found that nearly twice the number of young people there were diagnosed with a mental disorder in 2018 as compared to 2003. The World Health Organization estimates that by 2028, depression will be the second leading type of disability worldwide. It is clear that aspects of the modern world make it more difficult for people to maintain good mental health.
Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

main_body.text: The 21st century is witnessing a significant rise in the proportion of people being diagnosed by medical professionals as having a mental illness. For example, at the turn of the century, the number of Canadians being treated for depression increased by over 30% in just one year. A recent study in the US found that nearly twice the number of young people there were diagnosed with a mental disorder in 2018 as compared to 2003. The World Health Organization estimates that by 2028, depression will be the second leading type of disability worldwide. It is clear that aspects of the modern world make it more difficult for people to maintain good mental health.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is the best statement of the flaw in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Changes in health care and a decrease in stigma attached to mental illness may be responsible for higher diagnosis rates.

options.label: B
options.text: Many people with a mental health diagnosis may be able to function well in society.

options.label: C
options.text: Significant numbers of people may be hesitant to seek help for mental health concerns from doctors or other medical professionals.

options.label: D
options.text: Some physical and behavioural factors may make mental health diagnoses more difficult.

options.label: E
options.text: In some cultures people may prefer to seek help for mental health concerns from religious leaders as opposed to doctors.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The main conclusion of the argument is contained in the final sentence: aspects of the modern world
make it more difficult for people to maintain good mental health. The evidence for this conclusion is
that diagnoses of depression have been increasing in recent years (reflected in the statistics from
Canada and America).

The problem with this reasoning is that a rise in diagnoses does not in itself tell us that the incidence
of depression is increasing. It is possible that the number of people suffering from depression has
remained fairly constant; it may just be that more of these people are coming forward because of
reduced social stigma and that changes in health care are picking up more cases. This is expressed
in option A.

Option B suggests a reason to moderate concern about the rise in diagnoses of depression. But this
is irrelevant because the point of the argument is to explain why there has been an increase as
opposed to judging how concerned we should be about it.

Option C suggests a reason for thinking the incidence of depression might exceed the number of
diagnoses. If this were the case, then, with certain other assumptions, option C would provide some
support for the conclusion.

Option D, like option C, suggests a possible obstacle to our getting an accurate picture of people’s
mental health. If diagnosis is difficult, then more people may be suffering from depression than we
know about. Again, this might be said to support the conclusion.

Option E raises a possibility that could be used to criticise the strategy of the argument. If some
people with mental health conditions seek help from their religious leaders, statistics from the health
service may not provide a reliable picture of how many people suffer from depression.

question_view.question_text:
In the UK we are increasingly engrossed by entertainment: we devote more time to it than sleep and spend more money on it than food and drink. The aim of entertainment is to create a make-believe situation in which emotions can be excited and discharged without affecting real life. While entertainment has its proper place, it can become a preoccupation, dominating our thoughts and sapping our emotional energy. When this happens, the ‘real’ world of action starts to appear comparatively dull and tedious and this, in turn, undermines social cohesion.
Our increasing use of entertainment is, then, threatening our wellbeing.
Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

main_body.text:
In the UK we are increasingly engrossed by entertainment: we devote more time to it than sleep and spend more money on it than food and drink. The aim of entertainment is to create a make-believe situation in which emotions can be excited and discharged without affecting real life. While entertainment has its proper place, it can become a preoccupation, dominating our thoughts and sapping our emotional energy. When this happens, the ‘real’ world of action starts to appear comparatively dull and tedious and this, in turn, undermines social cohesion.
Our increasing use of entertainment is, then, threatening our wellbeing.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following is an underlying assumption of the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Our wellbeing depends on social cohesion.

options.label: B
options.text: People prefer entertainment to food and drink.

options.label: C
options.text: Viewers copy the behaviour they see in entertainment media.

options.label: D
options.text: Emotions pose a threat to society.

options.label: E
options.text: The general public are addicted to entertainment.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The main conclusion of the argument is stated in the final sentence: our increasing use of
entertainment is threatening our wellbeing. This is inferred from two claims. The first is that if we’re
preoccupied with entertainment, it can dominate our thoughts and sap our emotional energy. The
second is that if entertainment dominates our thoughts and saps our emotional energy, the ‘real’ world
is likely to appear dull and tedious – making us less socially cohesive.

But the conclusion only follows if there is a connection between social cohesiveness and wellbeing.
Option A supplies this connection: our happiness or wellbeing depends on people engaging with the
real world and being socially cohesive. The line of reasoning in option A is essential for the conclusion
to be drawn.

Option B picks up on our relative expenditure on food, drink and entertainment, but this is beside the
point. The connection between the increased consumption of amusements and social disintegration
can be made without assuming any order of preference.

Although the argument raises a problem about people’s use of entertainment, the issue has nothing to
do with fears about ‘copycat’ behaviours. So the argument does not need to assume option C.

The argument does not depend on option D because it focuses on people who feel that the ‘real’
world is relatively uninteresting, which is distinct from any fundamental incompatibility of emotion and
society.

Option E is a statement about the extent of the public’s engrossment in entertainment. It is an (invalid)
intermediate conclusion which goes too far from the statements given in support.

Adults over the age of 60 are often depicted by the media as depressed, lonely and grumpy.
Of course, old age is associated with physical decline, health issues become more common and memory gets fuzzier. Previously, theories of ageing assumed that emotional experiences would follow a similar pathway towards dysfunction. They were wrong. Recent research has shown that in old age negative emotions (like anger) wane, while positive emotions (like contentment) become more common. Why? Our lives undergo pronounced changes in later life. Work demands are eliminated, there is more time for leisure pursuits, and older people structure their environments in ways that reduce unnecessary stress. Time horizons shrink:
people learn to spend their remaining precious time on the things that matter most.
Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

main_body.text:
Adults over the age of 60 are often depicted by the media as depressed, lonely and grumpy.
Of course, old age is associated with physical decline, health issues become more common and memory gets fuzzier. Previously, theories of ageing assumed that emotional experiences would follow a similar pathway towards dysfunction. They were wrong. Recent research has shown that in old age negative emotions (like anger) wane, while positive emotions (like contentment) become more common. Why? Our lives undergo pronounced changes in later life. Work demands are eliminated, there is more time for leisure pursuits, and older people structure their environments in ways that reduce unnecessary stress. Time horizons shrink:
people learn to spend their remaining precious time on the things that matter most.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Not everyone experiences the negative physical decline in old age often depicted in the media.

options.label: B
options.text: In old age people experience both positive and negative emotions less strongly.

options.label: C
options.text: Being freed from the demands of work allows retired people to feel happier.

options.label: D
options.text: Older people find better ways of avoiding stress and using their time productively.

options.label: E
options.text: Assumptions that the emotional aspects of ageing mirror the physical aspects were wrong.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The main conclusion of the argument is that it was wrong to assume that the physical decline
associated with ageing is mirrored by an emotional decline.

The evidence for this conclusion is that recent research shows that negative emotions wane in old
age and positive emotions are more common.

The passage provides an explanation for this reasoning:

‘Work demands are eliminated, there is more time for leisure pursuits, and older people structure their
environments in ways that reduce unnecessary stress. Time horizons shrink: people learn to spend
their remaining precious time on the things that matter most.’

Option E expresses the main conclusion.

Option A conflates the claim made in the first sentence (that the media show old people as being
‘depressed, lonely and grumpy’) with the fact accepted in the second sentence that physical decline is
associated with old age. The argument is that the media portrayal of older people’s mental states is
inaccurate.

Option B misrepresents the statement in the passage in sentence 5, which says that negative
emotions wane but positive emotions become more common. It is this change in the balance of
positive and negative emotions which supports the main conclusion that portrayal of elderly people is
unduly negative.

Options C and D provide explanations for the change in the balance of emotions.

Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

main_body.text: You are allowed to vote in the general election only if you are at least 18 years old. You have reached 18 so you will be able to vote in the forthcoming election.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: You cannot obtain foreign currency from this bank if you cannot produce acceptable identification. You cannot produce the required identification, therefore we cannot let you have the foreign currency.

options.label: B
options.text: You can visit your grandmother in hospital providing you have no illness yourself. As you have no illness, you will be able to visit your grandmother.

options.label: C
options.text: We can afford to go to America this year only if you save up sufficient money. You haven’t saved enough so we will not be able to go.

options.label: D
options.text: To win the jackpot prize in the national lottery you need a ticket with all six prize-winning numbers. When I heard you had won the jackpot, I knew you had the lucky ticket that matched all the numbers from the draw.

options.label: E
options.text: Passport applications can only be accepted if photographs are witnessed as a likeness by someone in a professional job. Your application was refused so your witness cannot have been a professional person.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The passage and option B share the same underlying structure: P is necessary for Q; P is true;
therefore Q must be true.

In the passage: P = ‘You are 18 years old’ and Q = ‘You can vote in the general election’.
In option B: P = ‘You are not ill’ and Q = ‘You can visit your grandmother in hospital’.

Option A has the underlying structure: P is necessary for Q; P is not true; therefore Q is not true.
P = ‘You can produce acceptable identification’ and Q = ‘You can obtain foreign currency’.

Option C has the underlying structure: P is necessary for Q; P is not true; therefore Q is not true.
P = ‘You have saved up sufficient money’ and Q = ‘We can go to America this year’.

Option D has the underlying structure: P is necessary for Q; Q is true; therefore P must be true.
P = ‘You have a ticket with all six prize-winning numbers’ and Q = ‘You win/won the jackpot in the
lottery’.

Option E has the underlying structure: P is necessary for Q; Q is not true; therefore P is not true.
P = ‘Photograph is witnessed as a likeness by someone in a professional job’ and Q = ‘A passport
application is accepted’.

question_view.question_text:
Microscopic malaria parasites enter a person’s bloodstream through mosquito bites and infect red blood cells. They replicate in these cells and penetrate other organs. Until recently, microbiologists sought to block the parasites from entering red blood cells. Rhode Island University studied 700 Tanzanian children infected with malaria and found the parasites use a protein, since named PfSEA-1, to escape from the red blood cells they infect. Having investigated a subgroup of children immune to malaria, the researchers realised these children were producing an antibody that locked protein PfSEA-1 into their red blood cells. Trapped in the red cells, the parasites were destroyed by immune system cells. Scientists have reproduced the antibody and successfully tested it on mice. Experts believe that, after trials, the antibody will be certified for use in the treatment of humans.
Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?

main_body.text: Microscopic malaria parasites enter a person’s bloodstream through mosquito bites and infect red blood cells. They replicate in these cells and penetrate other organs. Until recently, microbiologists sought to block the parasites from entering red blood cells. Rhode Island University studied 700 Tanzanian children infected with malaria and found the parasites use a protein, since named PfSEA-1, to escape from the red blood cells they infect. Having investigated a subgroup of children immune to malaria, the researchers realised these children were producing an antibody that locked protein PfSEA-1 into their red blood cells. Trapped in the red cells, the parasites were destroyed by immune system cells. Scientists have reproduced the antibody and successfully tested it on mice. Experts believe that, after trials, the antibody will be certified for use in the treatment of humans.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?

options.label: A
options.text: Rhode Island University is a world leader in medical research.

options.label: B
options.text: After the discovery of protein PfSEA-1, the traditional approaches to fight malaria will be abandoned as ineffective.

options.label: C
options.text: The discovery of protein PfSEA-1 is likely to help scientists to develop a new way of combatting malaria.

options.label: D
options.text:
World leaders should support and fund the research being conducted by Rhode Island
University.

options.label: E
options.text: A unique feature of the Tanzanian children helped in the discovery of protein PfSEA-1 and its function in spreading malaria.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The passage describes a new method for preventing the replication of malaria parasites in red blood
cells. The PfSEA-1 protein prevents malaria parasites from escaping from the blood cells they
penetrate and they are subsequently eliminated by the immune system. Researchers discovered that
a group of children immune to malaria had an antibody that prevented malaria parasites from
accessing the PfSEA-1 protein.

From this information we can draw option C as a conclusion. If it’s true (and sentences 4 and 5 tell us
this) that the antibody limits malaria parasites’ access to a crucial protein, then the ability to reproduce
the antibody in a form that could be given to patients promises a treatment against malaria.

We cannot draw option A as a conclusion because although Rhode Island University carried out the
promising research, it doesn’t follow that the institution is necessarily a world leader in medical
research.

We cannot draw option B as a conclusion because the development of a new treatment for malaria
does not mean doctors will automatically abandon existing therapies.

We cannot draw option D as a conclusion because the passage does not make any specific claims
about what world leaders ought to support and fund. This option goes beyond the factual information
in the passage without support.

We cannot draw option E as a conclusion because the passage does not provide further information
about whether what was found in the blood cells of the immune Tanzanian children was unusual or
not.

question_view.question_text:
Despite the government’s promise to be more business friendly, plans have been announced to change the law regarding the paid leave that couples are entitled to take following the birth of a child. This will allow new parents to take more time off work than under the current regulations. It is claimed that the current legislation makes it difficult for those with family commitments to manage all of their responsibilities, but it needs to be recognised that businesses (and in particular small businesses) need to operate in a way that guarantees that staff are available to do the jobs that need doing. The new proposals are undoubtedly going to make the system more complicated and could dissuade businesses from employing certain groups of people. They should be opposed.
Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

main_body.text: Despite the government’s promise to be more business friendly, plans have been announced to change the law regarding the paid leave that couples are entitled to take following the birth of a child. This will allow new parents to take more time off work than under the current regulations. It is claimed that the current legislation makes it difficult for those with family commitments to manage all of their responsibilities, but it needs to be recognised that businesses (and in particular small businesses) need to operate in a way that guarantees that staff are available to do the jobs that need doing. The new proposals are undoubtedly going to make the system more complicated and could dissuade businesses from employing certain groups of people. They should be opposed.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The example given is only one of a range of measures being proposed.

options.label: B
options.text: Many businesses now allow their employees to choose to work from home.

options.label: C
options.text: The proposals from the government provide support for businesses to help with the cost of covering the work of staff taking leave.

options.label: D
options.text: The problems associated with covering the work of absent members of staff become increasingly difficult the longer the absence goes on.

options.label: E
options.text: The proposals will increase the amount of leave that employees are allowed to take in other circumstances as well as following the birth of a child.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The main conclusion of the argument is that new proposals to increase the entitlement to paid leave
following the birth of a child should be opposed. The basis for this conclusion is that certainty around
staffing is necessary for businesses to operate. Since the proposal would extend leave for new
parents, the author draws the intermediate conclusion that the change would make staffing more
complicated and might lead to discriminatory recruitment practices.

Option C weakens the inference to the intermediate conclusion: if the proposal includes support from
government to help with covering leave, the negative effects on businesses are not inevitable.

Option A does not weaken the argument because it is focused on the effect of extending parental
leave and not on any of the other measures being proposed.

Option B does not weaken the argument because the issue is not where employees are working, but
whether businesses have staff available to do the work at all.

Option D has the potential to strengthen the argument: if the negative effect of leave increases with its
duration, the proposed extension of parental leave may be more problematic than the existing
arrangements.

Option E provides a further reason to reject the plans. The threat to business certainty may be greater
if employees are entitled to take leave in a broader range of circumstances than at present.

As long as there is the right combination of guests, any party will be a success. The last party was great, so there must have been a perfect selection of guests.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?

options.label: A
options.text: As long as there is a high level of unemployment, all economies will perform below their maximum potential. Unemployment levels here have risen sharply, so our economy will perform less well than it could do.

options.label: B
options.text: As long as there are good hotels, any seaside town can get on the tourist trail. Our town is a tourist hotspot, yet none of the hotels are any good.

options.label: C
options.text: As long as there is somebody in charge, any project will go smoothly. James has taken firm control, so this week’s project will be fine.

options.label: D
options.text: As long as there are lots of security personnel around, public order is sure to be maintained. We have been having huge problems with public disorder here, so there cannot be many security people.

options.label: E
options.text: As long as there is lots of water, any habitat will support life. Life is abundant in that habitat, so there must be lots of water.

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The passage and option E both share the same underlying structure: If P then Q; Q is true; therefore
P must be true.

In the passage: P = ‘the right combination of guests’ and Q = ‘the party will be a success’.
In option E: P = ‘there is lots of water’ and Q = ‘a habitat will support life’.

Option A has the underlying structure: If P then Q; P is true; therefore Q must be true.
P = ‘high levels of unemployment’ and Q = ‘the economy performs less well’.

Option B has the underlying structure: If P then Q; Q is true and P is not true.
P = ‘there are good hotels’ and Q = ‘a seaside town will be popular’.

Option C has the underlying structure: If P then Q; P is true; therefore Q must be true.
P = ‘someone is in charge’ and Q = ‘the project will go smoothly’.

Option D has the underlying structure: If P then Q; Q is not true; therefore P must not be true.
P = ‘security personnel are around’ and Q = ‘public order is maintained’.

main_body.text:
A builder has 32kg of a mix of sand and cement, of which 25% is sand. For a new job, he
:
needs 120kg of a mix of sand and cement in which the ratio of sand to cement is 2 1. To obtain this, he starts with his initial 32kg mix and adds more sand and cement.

question_view.main_question: What is the ratio of the masses of sand and cement that he needs to add?

notes: Rendered from original PDF; coordinates use top-left PDF points.

blocks.text:
The builder has 32 kg of a mix made up of 8 kg of sand (25%) and therefore 24 kg of cement.
He needs his final mix to be 120 kg, made up of 80 kg of sand and 40 kg of cement (2 : 1 ratio).
This means that he needs to add 72 kg of sand and 16 kg of cement to his original mix. This is a ratio
of 72 : 16, which, in simplest terms, is 9 : 2. The correct answer is option D.

Although the Scottish Government has announced plans to ban corporal punishment of children (smacking), we must preserve the right of parents in the rest of the UK to smack their children when it is reasonable. This is not because we are violent people eager to hit our kids:
we recognise that smacking is damaging to children. The point is rather that people resent being legislatively compelled to do what they would have done anyway. It only breeds contempt for the law and since the wellbeing of citizens depends on people respecting the law, we should take steps to prevent it falling into disrepute. We must, therefore, protect the rights of parents in Northern Ireland, Wales and England to smack their children.
Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

main_body.text:
Although the Scottish Government has announced plans to ban corporal punishment of children (smacking), we must preserve the right of parents in the rest of the UK to smack their children when it is reasonable. This is not because we are violent people eager to hit our kids:
we recognise that smacking is damaging to children. The point is rather that people resent being legislatively compelled to do what they would have done anyway. It only breeds contempt for the law and since the wellbeing of citizens depends on people respecting the law, we should take steps to prevent it falling into disrepute. We must, therefore, protect the rights of parents in Northern Ireland, Wales and England to smack their children.

question_view.main_question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Respect for the law is the decisive factor that underpins social cohesion in the UK.

options.label: C
options.text: The ban is one element in a larger mental and physical health programme for children being undertaken by the Scottish Government.

options.label: D
options.text: The damage caused by smacking far exceeds the damage caused by negative attitudes towards the law.

options.label: E
options.text: Popular opinion can, in some cases, be an effective constraint on immoral behaviour.

blocks.text:
The main conclusion of the argument is that parents in Northern Ireland, Wales and England should
retain the right to smack their children. The basis for this conclusion is that people resent being
compelled by law to do what they are inclined to do anyway. Any such resentment breeds contempt
for the law, which is a problem because the wellbeing of citizens depends on people respecting the
law.

Option D weakens the argument by introducing a further consideration to take into account: if
smacking is worse than negative attitudes towards the law, it is far from obvious that we should
prioritise respect for the law over the protection of children.

Option A is consistent with the claim in the passage that smacking is damaging to children and so
does not affect the argument.

Option B has the potential to strengthen the argument: if respect for the law is necessary for social
cohesion then there may be grounds to prioritise it.

Option C does not weaken the argument because the other aspects of the programme are distinct
from the effects of this specific ban.

Option E might strengthen the argument: if ‘peer pressure’ is as good as law in controlling behaviour,
there is perhaps less reason to enshrine the ban on smacking in law.

Sometimes we are mistreated by others, and forgiveness is one kind of response to those who wrong us. However, sometimes we do things that appear to be morally wrong but, in fact, are not. If we are reproached, we can give an explanation for our action that justifies it. In these cases, we are claiming that, despite appearances to the contrary, what we did was morally permissible. Forgiveness and justification ought to be distinguished. When conduct is justified, the implication is that it was not morally wrong, but when conduct is forgiven, there is no such implication. What we are forgiven for is the morally wrong things we do.
Which one of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the above argument?
